1o8odj8.text: A critical vulnerability dubbed Java4Shell in OpenJDK, the open-source implementation of Java, can allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code on popular enterprise applications, including Jenkins, Atlassian Jira, Confluence, and Keycloak. Java is one of the most widely used programming platforms in the world, powering enterprise applications, web services, financial systems, and critical business infrastructure. Because many applications use the same Java runtime, vulnerabilities in its core components can affect a wide range of different and unrelated applications. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, is a memory-corruption flaw in Java's hardware-accelerated Base64 decoding functionality that can be exploited to disclose sensitive information from memory or achieve remote code execution (RCE). Security researchers at Calif, who disclosed the flaw on Tuesday, rated it critical with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2, while Oracle assigned it a lower severity rating of 8.1 (High) using CVSS 3.1. Java4Shell affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later, as well as Java distributions built from the affected code, including Oracle Java SE, Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, and Red Hat OpenJDK. The vulnerability stems from a bug in Java's Base64 decoder, which processes encoded data commonly found in authentication, file uploads, and network communications. According to Calif, specially crafted Base64 data can cause the decoder to overwrite portions of Java's memory, potentially allowing attackers to steal sensitive information or execute malicious code. The researchers say that the memory corruption can be triggered with just 64 "A" characters followed by a single equals sign (=): AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA= Older OpenJDK 17 versions require 128 "A" characters followed by the equals sign. The flaw only affects a hardware-accelerated decoding function used on certain x86-64 processors that support AVX-512 instructions. The researchers have been able to exploit this bug to perform remote code execution against a variety of widely used Java applications running with their default configurations, including: Unauthenticated RCE: Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Authenticated RCE: Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker. Calif was also able to exploit the flaw in sample applications built using the Apache Struts and Spring Boot frameworks. However, the researchers said Java4Shell does not have a universal exploit, and attackers must find an application-dependent way to deliver malicious Base64 data to the vulnerable decoder to achieve code execution. The vulnerability also requires the affected hardware-accelerated AVX-512 decoding function to be used, which depends on supported x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI capabilities. Calif says researcher Quang Luong discovered the flaw using OpenAI's Codex AI coding assistant, which helped identify the vulnerability during an audit of OpenJDK's internals. According to the researchers, Luong discovered the flaw in approximately one hour and developed an initial working exploit in another two hours, at a total AI usage cost of less than $200. The company says AI agents also helped develop additional application-specific exploitation chains. Calif has published a proof-of-concept demonstrating the memory corruption but has not released the weaponized exploits used against the affected enterprise applications. Oracle released patches for CVE-2026-114938 on November 17 as part of its November Critical Security Patch Update, which addresses 655 security vulnerabilities across its product portfolio. The company recommends that customers apply the available security patches as soon as possible. For those who cannot immediately update their Java implementations, Calif recommends disabling the vulnerable hardware-accelerated Base64 functionality by launching OpenJDK with the -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics option. Alternatively, administrators running Java on x86-64 systems can use -XX:UseAVX=2 to disable AVX-512 instructions. However, these workarounds are temporary mitigations, and all developers should update the Java runtimes to the latest version. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 19lvkis.text: Credentials and access secrets exposed in public Docker Hub images are being extracted and exploited by attackers within as little as eight seconds of publication. Two researchers at Stony Brook University, Billy Tsouvalas and Nick Nikiforakis, measured the extraction speed by publishing a total of 300 honeypot images across eight public container registries. Over a period of four months, the researchers exposed AWS, OpenAI, and Anthropic API keys, along with decoy SSH and database credentials. They then monitored the use of these keys and placed detection tools to notify them when the images were built, ran, or had a shell opened. Honeypot experiment overview Source: containerbots.github.io The two researchers presented the experiment and the resulting findings yesterday at the ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS). They noted that their images were pulled more than 75,000 times, and the planted AWS keys received over 140,000 API calls from 5,000 unique IP addresses. The AWS traffic showed a broad pattern, from checking whether the keys worked to listing available resources, and sometimes proceeding to consume them. The fastest observed use of a planted AWS key came 7.86 seconds after the image was published on Docker Hub. The median time for the first API call was 51.19 seconds, while all 100 AWS keys were used within 15 minutes. API call times after image publication Source: containerbots.github.io The exposed OpenAI and Anthropic keys were quickly hijacked to exhaust the test-account balances. Docker Hub accounted for nearly all AWS activity, while Harbor, one of the other registries in the experiment, also saw some AWS key abuse. The researchers dubbed the automated scanners that interacted with their test images “ContainerBots,” though this is more of a loose umbrella term, as the scans showed no evidence of being coordinated by the same operators. Monitoring rarely detected anyone actually running the honeypot images, which led the authors to conclude that scanners generally extracted credentials by inspecting image layers directly. “The scanners interacting with our images overwhelmingly do so through static analysis, e.g., unpacking image layers or querying the registry API to extract filesystem contents, without ever instantiating the container,” explain the researchers. Exposing secrets this way is common in the real world [1, 2, 3], and revoking the leaked keys requires significant work and coordination. The researchers recommend that Docker Hub scans images for secrets before pushing them live, and warn publishers if they appear to embed any secrets. They also suggest restricting or rate-limiting access to Docker Hub’s public feed of recently published or updated images, to thwart mass-scanning tools. Tsouvalas told BleepingComputer that they reported their findings to Docker in May, along with the full paper, but besides an acknowledgment, they received no follow-up replies. A small-scale experiment they ran in August to determine whether any defenses had been implemented on the platform showed no changes. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. bi6n5e.text: A breach at a popular website management company exposed customers’ visitors to malicious code that stole cryptocurrency and attempted to skim payment cards or install malware. Researchers at cybersecurity firm Report URI said they found malicious JavaScript code on 178 different widely visited websites run through the Optimizely Web experimentation platform. Optimizely allows companies to personalize and manage their websites and apps. Optimizely confirmed the incident in a brief statement on Monday evening, writing that it “identified and contained a security incident affecting some Optimizely Web Experimentation customers.” “The vulnerable path is blocked, the injected code was removed, and customers have been contacted directly,” the company said. It did not respond to requests for comment about the specifics of Report URI’s study. In a technical advisory, Optimizely confirmed Report URI’s findings that a vulnerability in its Experimentation platform allowed threat actors to inject malicious JavaScript into some customers’ websites. Report URI listed dozens of prominent companies impacted by the breach and used blockchain evidence to track at least $7,000 stolen through the malicious code. “The malware was a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker's, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and on iPhones and iPads it delivered the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits. Crypto has already been stolen, with verified transactions to the attackers,” Report URI’s Scott Helme said. Most of the malicious code has now been removed, but Helme urged companies that use Optimizely to check their websites. Helme said the infected Optimizely files have all been cleaned since they reported the incident. Helme added that while they can track the stolen cryptocurrency, they have no way of seeing “how many credit cards were skimmed, how many cookies or screenshots were stolen, or how many iOS devices were infected before the attack was stopped.” The malicious code was installed on 32 finance or banking websites and several platforms for technology, news, airline and retail companies. Helme noted that they first saw the injected code on Turkish websites in September before the threat actor conducted its latest campaign on Monday. Coruna and Darksword Experts at cybersecurity firm Hudson Rock confirmed Report URI’s findings. Last week, threat hunting firm iVerify warned that cybercriminals are increasingly infecting devices on a large scale with spyware — with about 75% of detections involving criminal actors deploying Coruna or DarkSword exploit kits. DarkSword allows users to be infected without clicking on a link. Simply visiting a compromised website through a web browser can trigger an attack. Coruna is also delivered via web-based attacks, where people visiting malicious sites trigger WebKit and kernel vulnerabilities. Research from InfoStealers also found that poisoned third-party JavaScript has been actively routing iOS visitors into Coruna and DarkSword exploit-kit infrastructure. Collin Hogue-Spears, a cybersecurity expert at Black Duck, said companies typically use the affected Optimizely tool so that teams can change a live website without a code release. The attacker's loader went into Project JavaScript, the field where a customer adds custom code to Optimizely. “The Optimizely skimmer reads forms the affected sites built themselves; a payment processor's hosted iframe sits outside its reach, so security teams at affected companies must reconstruct which pages loaded the infected Optimizely snippet, for how long, and which card payments those pages took in that time period,” he said. “If the Optimizely skimmer ran unblocked on a page with your own card form, count as exposed every card entered there while the skimmer was live.” The incident resembles a recent incident impacting movie ticket site Fandango, which notified state regulators that payment card numbers, CVV numbers, expiration dates and more were stolen when hackers put malicious code into the sites' ticketing checkout page. No previous articleNo new articlesJonathan Greigis a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

n8rmol.text: The Fugaku supercomputer operated by Japan's RIKEN Center for Computational Science has been taken offline following a security breach. The organization says that between November 10 and 13, an unauthorized party exploited the public dashboard displaying Fugaku's operational status to gain access to multiple internal servers. Although the research center has yet to determine the access method, RIKEN’s investigation confirmed that the intruder accessed some servers to plant malware that targeted user data. Specifically, the organization says that the following details have been compromised: Names, email addresses, and user IDs of 4,222 Fugaku users Names and email addresses of 375 Rikyu users SSH private keys and access keys stored on users’ computers Research data files stored on users’ computers RIKEN notes that the attacker used some of the access keys in attempts to connect to additional systems, but the investigation did not determine further unauthorized access or theft of research results. The organization has not attributed the attack, and it’s still working to determine the exact intrusion method. RIKEN’s Center for Computational Science operates the two supercomputers, making them available to researchers in academia and industry sectors. Fugaku, which entered shared use in March 2021, is a 537 petaflops supercomputer used in drug discovery, severe-weather forecasting, and simulations of airborne virus transmission. Rikyu is a 64 petaflops supercomputer used in AI scientific research. In response to the incident, RIKEN shut down Fugaku on November 14, disabled users’ login keys, and asked users to revoke and replace any credentials they had stored on the supercomputer. RIKEN said Fugaku operations will resume only after it has ensured that it’s safe to do so. The remediation effort includes addressing the exploited software vulnerability, rebuilding compromised servers, reviewing the network configuration, and implementing advanced AI-driven security measures. Users are advised to revoke any SSH keys and other credentials stored on Fugaku, and watch out for suspicious emails impersonating RIKEN. A RIKEN spokesperson told BleepingComputer that they have no more details to share about the incident at the time, but promised to publish updates when the investigation uncovers new findings. aui57k.text: A malicious widget can bypass the security filter that Telegram added to its Android app last week and run code outside it, according to NebuSec, a security company. Widgets are small interactive blocks that bots send inside chat messages, and their JavaScript runs on the user's phone. The researchers ran their demonstration on a Telegram test server, because only approved bots can send widgets on the live service now. Bots could start sending widgets last week. Two days later, an account called V12 posted a video on X claiming that any Telegram message could now be used to execute remote code. Telegram then put QuickJS, the small engine that runs widget JavaScript, into its own process on Android. It also added a seccomp filter, which can block or record the system calls that the process makes. Both changes appear in the source code it published for Telegram for Android 13.2.2 (7303). NebuSec said in a technical analysis published earlier this week that its researchers got code running outside that filter in two separate ways. One uses a widget bug the filter does not cover, and the other chains a widget bug the filter does cover with a kernel bug. In their video, a bot's Telegram widget on Android 13.2.2 (7303) bypasses the filter and opens the phone's calculator app, the researchers say. Their write-up and their demonstration post on X do not say what the code could reach beyond that, such as the app's messages or the rest of the phone. They also do not say whether the user had to start the bot or tap the widget first. The researchers are holding back the details for now. Their write-up names no CVE identifier and does not say whether the bugs were reported to the app's developers. The widget documentation says widgets run in a sandbox, with rules such as no network access. Those rules live in the engine's own code, the researchers say. A single use-after-free or out-of-bounds write bug in QuickJS lets a script read and write the process's memory, and then the rules no longer protect anything. The new filter names a few dozen system calls, such as ptrace, bpf, and mount, and lets every other call through. The filter's source code leaves ioctl unfiltered. The filter sits on top of Android's own limits on the engine process. One process also runs every widget, so a hijacked widget from one bot shares memory with the widgets of every other bot, the researchers say. In the published source code for Telegram for Android 13.2.2 (7303), that filter is set to an audit mode, The Hacker News found. In audit mode, it still blocks attempts to start new programs or processes, but it only records the other listed calls and lets them run. A comment above the setting says how long that will last: "Audit until the logs from the devices say the engine never makes them." The published code does not show whether the version people install uses the same setting. "Yes, currently, general bots aren't allowed to use widgets even in private chats," a contributor to the telegram-bot-api project wrote late last week in a bug report thread on GitHub. As of this week, no later message in the thread says which bots are still allowed or that the limit has been lifted. The researchers' write-up lists no fixed version, and the published Android source code is no newer than 13.2.2 (7303) as of this week. "No one could be hacked just by receiving a message," Pavel Durov, Telegram's chief executive, wrote late last week in a channel post. His post addressed reports of code execution through widgets in the Android and Windows apps, and came before the researchers' demonstration. He added that a user first had to start a third-party service, and that even that was fully patched on the server side. The company had earlier said that the problem in V12's first demonstration was fixed and that the fix had reached all users. Separately, the security vendor Kaspersky said late last week that it had detected suspected exploitation of a flaw in Telegram widgets when people visited some Telegram channels. In that activity, a PowerShell script ran without the user noticing and downloaded and launched WebRAT, also known as Salat Stealer. The malware allows attackers to control the infected system and steal data from crypto wallets and Telegram accounts. The vendor's malware warning does not identify the flaw or the Telegram version, does not report the number of victims, and does not link the activity to either demonstration. It advises not running widgets until a fix is released.

1w440j2.text: Apple is reporting service disruptions affecting several of its services, including iCloud Mail, iCloud Account & Sign In, Apple School Manager, and Schoolwork. According to Apple's System Status page, at least six services were experiencing issues or outages as of 2:10 PM ET on November 17, 2026. The most widespread issue affects iCloud Account & Sign In, which Apple lists as an ongoing issue affecting all users. The company warns that the service may be slow or unavailable. The disruption started at approximately 11:45 AM ET. Apple has also reported outages affecting iCloud Mail and iCloud Web Apps (iCloud.com). Both incidents started at around 2:03 PM ET, with some users unable to access the services. Apple School Manager, Schoolwork and AppleCare are also affected The problems aren't limited to iCloud. Apple School Manager and Schoolwork are also experiencing outages, with some users affected. Both incidents started at approximately 1:40 PM ET. l8ejwy.text: An affiliate of the INC and Lynx ransomware strains appeared in a Tennessee court on Monday after being extradited from Italy. Roman Khlynovskiy, a 43-year-old from Kazakhstan, is accused of launching ransomware attacks against U.S. schools, hospitals and companies. Khlynovskiy is facing a maximum penalty of 27 years in prison on computer fraud, money laundering, wire fraud, extortion and identity theft charges. Prosecutors accused him of being a member of a cybercriminal group called the “8-Digits Team” that launched ransomware attacks on behalf of the larger INC and Lynx ransomware gangs. The team’s cyber intrusions led to $500 million in ransom demands and they claimed to have stolen 50 terabytes of data consisting of more than 70 million confidential health records. FBI director Kash Patel said U.S. agencies worked with Italian law enforcement to extradite Khlynovskiy. “The defendant is charged with participating in one of the largest healthcare data breaches in decades,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva. “The indictment alleges a conspiracy that targeted hospitals and healthcare providers, stole vast quantities of sensitive patient information, and then sought to profit by threatening some of the most vulnerable members of our society. These alleged crimes exploited the deeply personal medical information of millions of people.” Khlynovskiy made his first federal court appearance in Knoxville, Tennessee, on Monday. Members of the 8-Digits Team attacked companies in at least six states, often targeting schools and hospitals. The hackers breached networks, stole data and extorted victims, demanding payments in exchange for not publishing the data. The INC ransomware gang took credit for a 2024 ransomware attack on prominent Michigan healthcare system McLaren Health Care — which was forced to cancel dozens of surgeries and operate without critical digital systems for days. The group also caused chaos last year with an attack on the Dutch conglomerate behind several major U.S. supermarket brands. The INC gang emerged in 2023 and attacked the State Bar of Texas, Yamaha Motor and printer manufacturer Xerox. According to Palo Alto Networks and Group-IB, INC either rebranded to Lynx or Lynx actors purchased the group’s source code. z19mtz.text: Both criminal and state-backed groups in China are leveraging AI tools for cyber espionage, vulnerability research and social media influence operations. Google released its latest AI Threat Tracker report on Monday, writing that threat actors are rapidly evolving their use of artificial intelligence in attacks — now leaning more heavily on autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks like Artex, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI and PentAGI to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity. While multiple countries — including Russia, Iran and North Korea — are using AI for nefarious purposes, few countries have matched China. Google researchers said they saw Chinese state-backed and financially motivated actors using AI tools for “reconnaissance, front-end scanning, researching targets across various sectors and geographies, and weaponizing exploits.” Incident responders saw Chinese contractors using large language models to translate and comb through tranches of stolen data that were eventually organized and sold to customers. Other Chinese actors are using AI platforms’ file-hosting infrastructure to stage archives of phishing lures and exfiltrate stolen data. Several different Chinese actors are also experimenting heavily with Artex — which was spotlighted on Friday by the FBI in an alert that drew alarm among cybersecurity experts. The tool was created by a Chinese researcher and allows any user to turn a large language model into a powerful hacking tool that can “automate multiple phases of cyber intrusions at machine speed, from reconnaissance through data exfiltration,” according to the FBI. Google said it found evidence that Chinese government groups are now developing their own version of Artex for “likely use in cyber espionage operations.” While Artex has garnered the most media coverage, Google said they have seen similar tools used in real attacks or tested by threat actors in private — including CAIRN, PentAGI, CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike AI. CAIRN allows AI agents to collaborate on breaching targets, often starting with a target’s IP address and ending with an operational objective. Google saw CAIRN used in intrusions of companies in the U.S. aerospace sector. Some threat actors used PentAGI to conduct “systematic reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against a wide range of organizations in Asia,” the researchers added. Vulnerability research and disinformation Google said multiple countries and vendors now routinely employ large language models to research new bugs, create fake content, manipulate SEO and generate influence content. The report cites one instance of Iranian government-backed actor APT42 using several large language models, including Google’s Gemini, to conduct targeted reconnaissance and social engineering attacks. North Korea has continued to deploy AI to support its IT worker campaign, using it to create resumes and supplement knowledge during job interviews. The researchers added that recent intrusions into cryptocurrency organizations in North America and Europe saw North Korean hackers use AI to create fake recruiter profiles on professional networking profiles. The fictitious personas then conducted ClickFix attacks — where hackers force victims to take actions on their device to fix problems that are not real. The tactic has been used widely by North Korean actors in multiple attacks on cryptocurrency companies and was recently spotlighted as part of a long-running campaign recently disrupted by the FBI. Google found another version of the scheme, with North Korean actors conducting ClickFix attacks and breaching a victim’s device, allowing them to pivot into internal code repositories to install code directly into the large language models the companies use. The hackers modified code so that when users started up Claude Code, it would automatically trigger the download of a backdoor researchers call SOMBERMEME. Threat actors are also using LLMs to automate labor- and time-intensive phases of vulnerability analysis, allowing them to quickly analyze patches to find bugs — dramatically reducing the window between patch disclosure and exploitation. Google said zero-day exploits rose significantly this year, going from eight per month in 2025 to 22 in the month of August. As an example, Google cited two vulnerabilities that emerged this summer affecting PaperCut print management servers. Researchers were able to generate working exploits for the bug within a day of their disclosure using LLMs. Researchers noted in their report that while AI tools have compressed attack timelines and allowed some threat actors to move at “machine speed,” they do generate significant forensic traffic and rely on recognizable identifiers, leaving behind distinct code-level traces. “While these artifacts increase the likelihood of detection and mitigation, these tools remain highly capable of achieving operational objectives,” Google said. “As the sophistication of these tools and underlying LLMs increases, we anticipate not only reduced human involvement in these operations but also increased stealth and sophistication of the activity.” No previous articleNo new articlesJonathan Greigis a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

8zih6z.text: A Lack of ownership verification on the Hugging Face platform allowed researchers to take control of Kokoro, a text-to-speech model used in projects from Google, NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, and Amazon Web Services. An attacker hijacking the account could use it as a distribution channel in supply-chain attacks, potentially leading to data theft or code execution. However, the researchers demonstrated a stealthier attack: they modified the model's weights so it produced audio that differed from the input text, without changing the underlying application code. Because only the weights change, there is no malicious code or signature for malware scanners to detect, the researchers say. "We changed what this model says by fine-tuning its neural weights. Same input text. Same voice file. Same configuration. Same inference code — not a single line touched in the application that runs it," said security researcher Alon Hertz. Kokoro is an open-weight model that converts text into speech. It supports multiple languages and has more than 50 voice presets. Although its developer, Hexgrad, has not pushed an update since April 2025, the project continues to be popular, with nearly 13 million monthly downloads on Hugging Face. The GitHub repository and the Python package on PyPI also went silent around the same time. Kokoro is supported by developer tools from Google, NVIDIA, and Intel, including software for voice agents and on-device speech synthesis. AMD and Amazon Web Services have also published guides demonstrating its use in AI-agent workflows. Hertz and his team took control of the Kokoro account on Hugging Face by simply registering the domain used by the original owner and resetting the login password. Over the past weekend, the researchers registered the “hexgrad.com” domain listed on Kokoro’s public DONATE.md file and used it to perform a password reset on the publisher’s account. They then ran a controlled test in which they modified Kokoro’s model weights in 87 seconds using a gaming GPU, causing the model to produce poisoned output. Hertz says the team tested the modified Kokoro model locally using its normal inference pipeline, but never uploaded the modified weights to Hugging Face, as that would likely put at risk many production systems depending on the model. The researcher underlines that an update would still carry all the hallmarks of a legitimate release, as tests from another account showed that Hugging Face would not flag anything as suspicious. Despite the takeover, the publisher appeared the same, just like the file delivery route, the format, and the architecture. File sizes would be similar, and the release would contain no malware. A broader trust problem The researcher notes that the supply-chain risk from compromised publisher accounts distributing altered weights via routine updates to systems that automatically fetch new revisions is significant. Kokoro was just a high-profile example the team used to highlight the issue. Hertz says even non-hijacked accounts could pose a risk, as anyone can curate an ostensibly legitimate image for a period of time, then push a malicious update at some point. “Hugging Face does not vet publishers. It doesn’t verify whether an account is still held by its original, legitimate owner — or by whoever quietly took it over last week. It doesn’t vet the models or datasets those accounts upload,” Hertz says. “The same unvetted weights and datasets flow through mirrors and converted versions, GitHub releases, package registries, deployment guides, and direct downloads across the entire open-model ecosystem,” added the researcher. Hertz reported the issue to Hugging Face, hoping for quick action, but received no response. BleepingComputer has also contacted Hugging Face for comments, but we have not received a response yet. i21f6y.text: The Tor Project has released a security update for its network relay software to increase defenses against an ongoing distributed denial-of-service attack that it says has overwhelmed relays and affected most operators. Tor version 0.4.9.17 includes a series of security fixes, including one the project described as especially important for relay denial-of-service defenses involving IPv6 handling. “This release comes in rapid response to the ongoing DDoS attack on the network, which has affected most relay operators,” the Tor Project said in its release announcement. The project said a massive ongoing flood of client circuits has overwhelmed relays across the privacy network, causing a problem that has been difficult to address. The project says this update includes a security fix to improve relay defenses against denial-of-service attacks. "One fix in particular is especially important for relay DoS defenses related to IPv6 handling," explains the project. Tor is working on additional defenses and expects to issue further releases in the near future. Relay operators are urged to upgrade to version 0.4.9.17 as soon as possible. The project said no additional action is required after installing the update. The announcement did not provide any other details as to who is behind the DDoS attacks or when they began. The Tor Project thanked relay operators for helping respond to the attack, pointing to active discussions on its tor-relays mailing list and asking operators to continue providing support. "Thank you to all… except our attacker(s)." Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 13vqk42.text: California’s data privacy regulator on Tuesday fined rental car giant Hertz $1.55 million for making it difficult for customers to protect their data and failing to honor consumers’ requests to opt out of having their information shared. Hertz agreed to the fine and said it would change its business practices, according to a court filing shared by the regulator, the California Privacy Protection Agency (CPPA). The car rental company allegedly broke state law by not processing opt-out preference signals, which are automated digital signals consumers send from their devices or browsers to notify websites not to sell or share their data. Hertz, which also owns the Dollar and Thrifty brands, allegedly did not tell consumers how it processed the signals and added “friction” to the opt-out process, according to a CPPA press release. A spokesperson for Hertz did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Hertz has agreed to quarterly testing and monitoring practices to ensure they are submitting the correct information to CPPA, reviewing all new tracking technologies and testing opt-out compliance, the press release said. “Businesses have been on notice for years that we expect them to listen when Californians say no to trackers,” Lara Kehoe Hoffman, Acting Deputy Director of Enforcement for CalPrivacy, said in a statement. CPPA also announced a separate settlement with outdoor clothing and accessories manufacturer CC Filson Co. on Tuesday. The company must pay a $218,000 fine and agree to stop all device-based sales and sharing of consumers’ personal information to advertising technology companies within 30 days. A spokesperson for CC Filson Co. did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

hx55g.text: The National Security Agency’s classified internal communications network is experiencing what is believed to be a technical issue, resulting in a delayed opening and staggered employee arrivals. The difficulties with the system, known as NSA Net, are not believed to be the result of a cyberattack, according to two people familiar with the ongoing situation. CNN first reported the development. The NSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. There has been a staggered arrival at agency headquarters, located at Fort Meade, Maryland, specifically because officials want to reduce the load of tens of thousands of personnel signing in the morning at the same time on the same network, one of these people told Recorded Future News. This same person noted that the system is not completely shut down, but is only providing intermittent service NSA backup centers located around the country are expected to pick up the slack caused by the delays. Editor's Note: This story will be updated as more information becomes available.

mdd57e.text: Flipper Devices, the company behind the popular Flipper Zero pentesting device, has launched a crowdfunding campaign for Flipper One, a portable Linux computer and networking multi-tool. Despite global RAM shortages and unpredictable price fluctuations, the company said Flipper One will launch at $399, a price that reportedly covers production costs and leaves no profit margin. Flipper Devices said the device’s RAM and UFS storage account for half of the total hardware cost, but after years of development, they decided not to hold back now. “Instead of waiting for perfect market conditions or raising the price, we’re moving forward with the Kickstarter campaign,” reads the press release Flipper Devices shared with BleepingComputer. “We aim to make Flipper One as accessible as possible without building a profit margin into the hardware's price.” Flipper One is a portable computer that runs a Debian-based system called Flipper OS, and features built-in Wi-Fi 6E, Gigabit Ethernet, and an eSIM. Source: Flipper Devices It can manage up to five network uplinks, act as a hotspot, run VPNs and firewalls, and connect to an external display over USB-C. It is a separate product from Flipper Zero, focused on IP networking and on-device computing. In May, Flipper Devices asked the community to help build it, highlighting the project's complexity and listing several ambitious goals. Development appears to have progressed at a good pace since then, and the company is now preparing to build the first actual units of the Flipper One. The company says that Flipper One already runs on the mainline Linux kernel, while USB-C DisplayPort patches are under review for inclusion in the mainline Linux. Work continues on memory power efficiency and removing the remaining closed-source boot components. The campaign also offers LoRa (support for MeshCore, Meshtastic, Reticulum, and walkie-talkie mode), a 5G modem, and software-defined radio expansion modules (full specifications to be disclosed). Source: Flipper Devices The Kickstarter campaign for Flipper One will run between November 17 and December 17, with the goal of funding the first production run. Device shipment for the first buyers is estimated for July 2027, and the package will include the device and a USB-C cable. Flipper Devices also relied on Kickstarter to launch its iconic Flipper Zero in 2020, since then selling over 1 million devices. Flipper Zero reached its funding goal within eight minutes and raised $4.8 million from crowdfunding in 30 days. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss.
