ukjh1b.text: Oracle is preparing to release security patches for 11 vulnerabilities in Java SE on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, all of which may be exploited remotely without authentication, as separate reports warn of a potentially critical remote code execution (RCE) flaw affecting OpenJDK. The 11 vulnerabilities carry a maximum CVSS 3.1 severity score of 8.1, according to Oracle's advance security notice. The company has not disclosed their CVE identifiers, affected components, or the individual consequences of exploitation. The separate OpenJDK vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, has reportedly been assigned a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 and affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later. However, those details remain unconfirmed, and there is no evidence yet that the reported flaw is among the 11 vulnerabilities Oracle plans to patch. Security firm Calif said in a post on X that it discovered and reported the flaw, which it calls Java4Shell, and that the vulnerability had leaked. Calif said it would publish technical details by 1 p.m. Pacific time on November 17, after Oracle releases a patch. Security company watchTowr acknowledged the reports in a post on X, but cautioned that the technical details were still unconfirmed. Separate analyses of the OpenJDK source code by security companies Upwind and Equixly point to a flaw in Java's Base64 decoder whose likely result is a crash of the Java virtual machine (JVM) rather than code execution. The vulnerability's CVE record remains reserved without a public description. No official advisory has specified the vulnerable component, precise exploitation requirements, affected version range, or the availability of a fix. Oracle's ops.java site now lists the replacement builds below as its current releases. Oracle's advance notice, release notes and download page still showed the earlier builds as of 16:59 UTC. Oracle Prepares Java Security Updates Oracle advises customers to stop using its current builds of Java 8, 11, 17, 21, 25, and 27 after the November 17 security update and move to the corresponding replacement releases. The company's Java release notes contain the update guidance, while ops.java lists the following planned builds: Java line Current build Planned build Java 8 8u511 b33 8u513 Java 11 11.0.33.0.3 11.0.33.1 Java 17 17.0.21.0.3 17.0.21.1 Java 21 21.0.13.0.3 21.0.13.1 Java 25 25.0.5.0.3 25.0.5.1 Java 27 27.0.1.0.3 27.0.1.1 The November security notice identifies the following affected Oracle products and versions: Oracle Java SE: 8u511, 8u511-perf, 11.0.33, 17.0.21, 21.0.13, 25.0.5, and 27.0.1. Oracle GraalVM for JDK: 17.0.21 and 21.0.13. Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition: 21.3.20.0.3. Oracle JavaFX: 21.0.13, 25.0.5, and 27.0.1. Oracle says all 11 Java SE vulnerabilities may be exploited over a network without requiring credentials. That does not necessarily mean they all allow remote code execution or that every application running an affected Java version can be attacked directly. The advance notice does not identify the vulnerable Java components or specify what an attacker could accomplish by exploiting each flaw. Oracle also warns that the information may change before the complete security advisory is published. Critical OpenJDK RCE Report Remains Unverified The reported CVE-2026-114938 vulnerability introduces a separate concern for organizations operating Java applications, particularly those exposed to the internet. However, the public information does not establish whether the flaw affects the Java runtime itself, a particular library, or functionality that applications must expose for exploitation to succeed. However, Oracle's notice and the OpenJDK advisories do not establish whether the flaw affects the Java runtime itself, a particular library, or functionality that applications must expose for exploitation to succeed. Upwind said in a technical analysis that its reading of the OpenJDK source points to a flaw in Java's AVX-512 Base64 decoder, and Equixly reached the same finding in a separate analysis. The flawed code runs only on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI support, when untrusted data reaches the basic or URL decoder of java.util.Base64. ARM servers do not run it. The code is in Java 17.0.6 and later and in Java 21, 25 and 27, but not in standard Java 8 or 11. A crash is the likely result because the bytes written past the buffer are fixed and not chosen by the attacker. Neither firm reported reproducing the overflow on AVX-512 hardware. Oracle's 8u371-perf release notes show that its Java 8 Enterprise Performance Pack added a "Base64 Decoding optimization for x86 using AVX-512". Neither firm said whether the Performance Pack is affected. Both firms named two JVM options as stopgaps to keep the flawed code from running: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, which turns off the Base64 intrinsics, and -XX:UseAVX=2, which turns off all AVX-512 code paths and can slow other work. Neither option has been confirmed by a vendor for this flaw, the firms said. Oracle's November notice covers Oracle products and does not establish the patch status of third-party OpenJDK distributions. The OpenJDK Vulnerability Group, which coordinates security disclosures affecting OpenJDK source code, had not published an advisory newer than October 24 at the time of the earlier review. Until official details are available, organizations cannot determine from the reported CVE alone whether their Java deployments are vulnerable or which specific update addresses the issue. Oracle began a monthly security patch cycle on May 28, introducing targeted security releases between its quarterly Critical Patch Updates. Its Java security update plan, last updated September 10, identified November 17 as the next scheduled monthly release. Organizations should inventory deployed Java runtimes, identify internet-facing applications, and prepare to test and install the relevant vendor updates once they become available. This is a developing story. We will update this article as Oracle publishes its full vulnerability advisory and additional verified details about CVE-2026-114938, affected versions, and available patches emerge.

1bvv2h5.text: Artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, and logistics sectors across Europe and the U.S. have emerged as the target of a large-scale, industrialized campaign dubbed Trigram. "Trigram is a large-scale campaign that impersonates about 50 brands in the blockchain and AI sectors, to trick developers into executing an infostealer themselves," Stormshield said in a deep-dive technical report published Monday. "Three social engineering scenarios (recruitment, conference, and package tracking), a software supply-chain compromise, and trojanized code repositories all converge on the same infrastructure and the same payload." The activity is assessed to share similarities with intrusion sets linked to North Korea, particularly Kimsuky and UNK_DeadDrop. Some aspects of this campaign have been previously documented by Proofpoint, SafeDep, Jamf, and Genians Security Center. It's worth noting that the cluster tracked as UNK_DeadDrop exhibits similarities with a long-running North Korea-aligned campaign referred to as Contagious Interview. It employs phishing emails using developer role recruitment or code review themes to target developers across finance, cryptocurrency, education, and technology sectors to deploy an information stealer. On Linux and macOS systems, the attack chains lead to the deployment of Overlord, an open-source remote access trojan (RAT) framework to facilitate data theft. Then, in August 2026, Jamf Threat Labs disclosed details of a macOS campaign using a fake Zoom installer to deploy Overlord RAT, although the Apple device management company said at the time that it found no "direct overlap" between the activity and UNK_DeadDrop. "The Overlord variant observed here shares a LaunchAgent label (com.zoom) and plist name (com.zoom.plist) with FlexibleFerret, a DPRK-attributed macOS malware family associated with the Contagious Interview campaign," it added. Overlord has also been distributed as recently as late October 2026 via another channel: a forged commit in the antd-img-crop GitHub repository that installs the malware by means of a prebuild hook ("prebuild.js") as soon as a developer runs the "npm run build" command. The npm package in itself was not impacted. The JavaScript payload is designed to download and run a fake installer that sets up Node.js and fetches an encrypted JavaScript next-stage that runs entirely in memory and locates its command-and-control (C2) server via a GitLab dead drop. The third-stage malware is responsible for harvesting credentials and installing the OverLord framework. "The malware steals browser passwords, cookies, keychains, cryptocurrency wallets, SSH keys and .env files on macOS, Linux and Windows, then installs a remote-access agent disguised as Google software," SafeDep said in an analysis of the malware. The forged commit pushed to "antd-img-crop⁠" on October 31, 2026 On macOS and Linux systems, it also displays a fake dialog asking users to enter their system password so as to "apply system updates and verify drivers and security settings." Interestingly, the same payload is delivered via two other initial access vectors - A fake careers portal impersonating Amber Group, a legitimate cryptocurrency firm A sideloaded Microsoft Visual Studio Code (VS Code) or Cursor extension named "google-dev-tools.google-update-support" that's likely launched via a coding assessment and deleted after it's run "The fake recruiter, the paste-a-command 'verification' step and the focus on developers and cryptocurrency holders match the publicly documented Contagious Interview campaign," SafeDep said. "The match rests on technique and does not prove who the operators are." The third branch of the campaign revolves around another cluster tracked by Genians as Operation GitPower. Attributed to the Kimsuky group, the activity involves operating local large language model (LLM) environments using Ollama and GPT4All to generate decoy documents and use them to target professionals and organizations in the fields of policy, academia, international cooperation, diplomacy, and security research. Present within the phishing email is a Windows Shortcut (LNK) that, once launched, runs PowerShell code designed to retrieve the lure document via GitHub's raw content service and open it, while stealthily downloading additional payloads like AsyncRAT in the background. Kimsuky's use of GitHub for C2 The campaign has since evolved to target Ukrainian experts in diplomacy, security, and international policy, utilizing international conference invitations and requests for analytical collaboration to elicit responses from targets and eventually distribute malware in the form of ZIP archives containing malicious LNK files. In at least one case, the phishing emails have been found to trick recipients into clicking on bogus links to harvest their Google account credentials under the pretext of joining a Zoom meeting via Gmail. Another method involves distributing a counterfeit version of a Zoom installer that, in addition to installing the legitimate app, runs malware designed to run arbitrary PowerShell scripts and send the results back. "This attack is particularly noteworthy as it indicates that Kimsuky has expanded its targeting scope beyond its traditional focus on South Korea to include key individuals in Ukraine," Genians noted last month, adding these efforts were mostly unsuccessful. "Kimsuky's attacks against Ukraine may be cyber espionage operations aimed at collecting information on the war, the extent of North Korean troop losses, developments in the questioning and handling of prisoners of war, and the details of consultations between South Korea and Ukraine." The latest findings from Stormshield merge together all of these separate findings into a single, cohesive picture - a toolset comprising a management platform, victim-tracking consoles, and email-delivery infrastructure. The attack chain is a single infection chain that's adapted for three environments - Send the target an email advertising a job opportunity, entice them into clicking a link, and initiate the "recruitment" process. The website masquerades as a recruitment platform where visitors can view job listings and submit job applications. In the background, the web page fingerprints the visitor and uses an IP address-based geofencing mechanism to lock out users from specific regions (possibly China). If access is restricted, users are served a stripped-down version of the home page without any ability to interact with it. If the "applicant" satisfies the filtering criteria, they are served an application form to enter their personal details. The user is then prompted to enter a referral (or invitation) code, indicating that the campaign is aimed at pre-identified targets rather than a broad audience. If the code is rejected, the site displays one of three messages: "Already used," "Locked to another IP," and "Invalid code." If the code is accepted, the candidate is served a confirmation message and is instructed to copy and run a command on the Linux terminal as part of a technical check. Once the command is run, it sends the "nonce" information displayed on the web page to a remote server via an HTTP POST request. No file or script is downloaded or executed on the victim machine at this stage. The web page, which is waiting for confirmation from the server, responds with an error message, stating: "Operation timeout. Please try again. Nonce Refreshed." The attack moves to the second stage when the web page displays the same verification screen but with a modified "Copy" button behavior that injects the malicious command directly into the victim's clipboard. The same pattern is observed even when the target uses the "Ctrl+C" keyboard shortcut to copy the command from the web page. The actual command that gets executed depends on the operating system - On Windows, it launches PowerShell to download and run a file named "v.cmd" On Linux, it launches bash shell to download and run a file named "u" On macOS, it launches bash shell to download and run a file named "verify_m” "These scripts act as loaders: they prepare the execution environment, retrieve the necessary components, and launch a JavaScript payload, install_guard.js, fetched from a remote server," the French cybersecurity company explained. Trigram dropper execution phase This preparatory stage also involves extracting a Base64-encoded script that configures the working directory, establishes a locking mechanism to prevent concurrent installations, and checks for an existing Node.js installation. If a compatible version (minimum version 18) is not found, it proceeds to download and install Node.js version 20.18.1 based on the infected host's operating system and its architecture. It then downloads "install_guard.js," which deploys an infostealer tasked with collecting system metadata, browser credentials, cryptocurrency wallets, and sensitive files present on the machine. The entire operation is powered by a multi-layered architecture comprising fake recruitment (like Amber Group), conference invitation, and package delivery sites; C2 servers that host the JavaScript and are fetched by means of a GitLab dead-drop; and the back office hosted on "170.205.30[.]27:8000" that enables campaign management and victim tracking via a platform called "rms-platform." The tracking console records every action undertaken by the user, while simultaneously keeping tabs on bot visitors and lookalike domains that have been taken down. Each "real visitor" is then rated "important," "moderate," or "useless," suggesting some sort of shortlisting based on their value. Further analysis of the API routes associated with "rms-platform" show that it's capable of identifying potential targets by scraping GitHub profiles, sending phishing emails, managing decoys, issuing access codes, viewing and exporting collected data, and cryptocurrency wallet monitoring. Trigram infrastructure architecture "These three levels rely on abused legitimate services: GitHub and GitLab for code and configuration hosting; Brevo, Resend, Mailgun, and Smartlead for email delivery; and FullStory for visitor session recording," Stormshield explained. "The tracking consoles are not standalone applications: they are delivered within the same JavaScript code as the decoys. The same bundle is served to all visitors, and a check on the hostname or URL path determines which interface is displayed." The technical indicators that point in the direction of UNK_DeadDrop and Kimsuky are listed below - eros1030109@gmail[.]com, a super-administrator account for the consoles that matches with an email address used in Operation GitPower. 0xapp123, a Medium account that discusses Web3 trends and lists "eros1030109@gmail.com" as the contact email address as far back as June 2022. silviattech1129_db_user, an identifier that appears as a username for a MongoDB database associated with "rms-platform" and in the history of the GitLab dead-drop file used in the "antd-img-crop" repository hijack as "silviattech1129." alexlopez-g/rms-platform, a backup GitHub repository hosting "rms-platform," with the user having contributed to a separate project named "Foxtopia-NFT/foxtopia-frontend" that includes a ".vscode/tasks.json" file mirroring tactics outlined in UNK_DeadDrop. The commit is signed with an email address "harper.danie95@gmail[.]com," which has been used to target designers on Contra with fake job offers. asteara[.]org, a domain flagged as "related infrastructure" for UNK_DeadDrop that has been used to host or serve the Trigram back office. pichi_finance_hr, a Telegram account that impersonates the human resources department of Pichi Finance, a decentralized finance (DeFi) platform that went offline in January 2025, and is likely used as a way to approach targets by posing as recruiters. "Based on these infrastructure and tooling overlaps, we assess with high confidence that Trigram represents a continuation of the UNK_DeadDrop cluster, while illustrating an evolution in its delivery tactics," Stormshield concluded. "Trigram stands out through the diversification of its initial access vectors and the remote retrieval of its final payload, rather than embedding it directly within the trojanized repository." "This system automates the targeting of users on GitHub, orchestrates massive phishing campaigns through four email providers, monitors the compromise of each victim in real time, and launders the stolen funds through cryptocurrency wallets."

1pfru08.text: It’s never been easier to steal credentials, thanks to a growing number of phishing kits that give aspiring attackers everything they need in one convenient interface. Some now come with admin dashboards and round-the-clock support, like a SaaS business, and they’re designed specifically to steal Microsoft 365 session tokens. Even entry-level attackers who replay a stolen token can end up in an active session where the login and MFA are already complete, with instant access to the victim’s cloud resources and email. Huntress researchers analyzed three of these modern phishing kits. This article breaks down how they capture and replay tokens and what defenders can do about it. What’s inside a phishing kit A phishing kit is a pre-packaged set of code and templates, with instructions for launching a phishing campaign and using the data it steals for malicious activity. Basic kits are often simple HTML and script files that spin up a single fake login page. More advanced kits feature admin dashboards that attackers use to track victims, modify phishing page content, and relay credentials in real time. To understand why these kits are so dangerous, it helps to look at how they turn phishing lures into usable sessions. 2026 Cyber Threat Report: State of Phishing Phishing has been around forever, but it’s not slowing down. It’s just getting sneakier. The Huntress State of Phishing report walks through the top phishing trends over the last year, from the lure themes and impersonated brands to the psychological tricks designed to slip past your defenses. And it shows you how to turn your people from a vulnerability into your strongest line of defense. Read Report When attackers pivot from passwords to sessions Phishing kits now give attackers usable authenticated sessions through three tradecraft techniques. In a device code phishing attack, the victim authenticates directly with the identity provider while the attacker quietly captures the resulting authorization and uses it. The flow reduces friction for attackers because the victim never types credentials into an unfamiliar page, so the entire experience feels like a normal sign-in. Figure 1: Device code phishing attack flow AitM attacks reveal the limitations of MFA; the threat actor relays the authentication flow in real time, either with a fake login page or by intercepting an exchange within the legitimate app. The victim completes the MFA prompt while the attacker captures the resulting session information. This is why successfully completed MFA does not make the session trustworthy on its own. Figure 2: Example of an AiTM attack Token theft is far more valuable to attackers than password theft. After an attacker gets their hands on a sign-in token, a phishing kit like Kali365 (which we’ll dig into below) can help them replay it into an active session, where they can access cloud resources and the victim’s email accounts. If you suspect replay, look past the original phishing page and investigate how the token was used. Figure 3: How attackers convert stolen tokens into useful sessions These techniques don’t live in isolation. In the last few months, Huntress has analyzed several advanced phishing kits targeting Microsoft 365 tokens, including EvilTokens, Knight Office, and Kali365. Three phishing kits targeting Microsoft 365 tokens In early 2026, Huntress discovered EvilTokens as part of a device code phishing campaign that abused the Railway Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) platform as a token-harvesting and replay engine. A joint effort between Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit and the FBI later in the year led to the arrest of one of its alleged operators. Knight Office is an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing kit that steals valid Microsoft 365 session tokens and feeds them into an operator console. Attackers can replay those sessions and set up persistence across tenant accounts. The third kit, Kali365, bundles a full Phishing as a Service (PhaaS) operation into a single control panel so operators can capture tokens through device code flows and reverse-proxy lures, replay them into live Microsoft 365 sessions, maintain access, and scale activity with built-in AI features. Kits like these help attackers walk away with persistent access, not just usernames and passwords. What every defender can do about token theft A single signal is only one piece of the attack. Follow the full sequence from the lure to authentication, token issuance or theft, device registration, and mailbox activity to understand identity compromise in your environment. Defenders can look for these signs of a stolen session: Start by checking for successful sign-ins from unfamiliar cloud infrastructure. Then hunt for device code authentication and automated token refresh. Review new devices, authentication methods, and mailbox activity. On the response side, keep these priorities in mind: Containment must address identity artifacts, not just the original lure. Revoke refresh tokens, then remove unauthorized devices and Windows Hello credentials. Restrict or block device code authentication where you can, and investigate mailbox access, forwarding rules, and outbound phishing. Keep going after containment. Monitor for replay or re-entry, and keep hunting after the original phishing domain disappears. Join us for Tradecraft Tuesday to dig into more attacker tradecraft like this with Huntress researchers. Sponsored and written by Huntress Labs.

1wvbpq4.text: The Hacker NewsNov 17, 2026Supply Chain Security / DevSecOps Pinning GitHub Actions to an exact version of their code, known as SHA pinning, has become the go-to defense against software supply chain attacks. Attackers have already found a way around it. In March 2026, the hackers who hijacked Trivy, a widely used open-source security scanner, planted malicious code that looked like it came from GitHub's official checkout tool. They even labeled it a security fix. Teams pinned to it would have passed every check. The trick works because GitHub lets copies of a project, called forks, share code with the original. In May, the same technique hit the popular actions-cool/issues-helper tool, stealing credentials from the pipelines that ran it. The lesson: pinning guarantees the code won't change, but not who wrote it. That gap is the focus of an upcoming webinar, GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning. If your team treats pinning as the finish line, save your seat to learn what it actually protects you from, and what it doesn't. Immutability Is Not Provenance Pinning earned its reputation. When the tj-actions/changed-files compromise repointed tags to a malicious commit across more than 23,000 repositories in March 2025, teams that had pinned to SHAs were unaffected. GitHub now lets administrators enforce pinning as an organization-wide policy, and few security teams argue against it. But a pinned SHA leaves three questions unanswered: Authorship: A SHA doesn't tell you who wrote the commit. Any fork commit can be pinned. Project membership: Org-level enforcement checks that a reference is a 40-character SHA, not that the commit actually lives in the upstream project. Runtime: A Docker-based action pinned to a SHA can still build its image at runtime, pulling in dependencies that were never frozen. With agentic development pushing more code through CI than ever, each of those gaps gets exercised more often and reviewed less closely. GitHub's Lockfiles Help. They Don't Finish the Job. GitHub's 2026 Actions security roadmap, published March 26, put deterministic dependency locking front and center. Workflow lockfiles entered public preview on October 14 and became generally available on October 28, 2026. They tie every run to recorded commits for actions and their transitive dependencies, even if a tag moves later. That's real progress. Locked commits must exist on a branch of the source repository, which blunts fork-only impostors. But GitHub's own changelog is clear that locking "does not determine whether the dependency itself is safe." Commit authorship and runtime builds remain open; immutable releases only help when maintainers opt in, and lockfiles aren't currently supported on GitHub Enterprise Server. Not sure where your pipelines fall in that gap? Register for the webinar for a clear-eyed breakdown of what GitHub's roadmap fixes and what it still leaves to you. What You'll Learn Led by Erika Heidi, Staff Developer Relations Engineer at Chainguard, the session draws a hard line between immutability and provenance, and covers: What org-level pin enforcement actually verifies, and the false confidence it can create How impostor commits work, and why GitHub's repository network makes them possible What GitHub's Actions roadmap addresses, and what it doesn't Other ways to close the trust gap, including a curated catalog of vetted actions Who Should Attend Platform and DevOps engineers who own CI/CD, AppSec and DevSecOps teams writing pipeline policy, and security leaders who signed off on SHA pinning as "done." If your workflows pull in third-party actions, this session is for you. Attackers have already shown they can disguise a malicious commit as a hardening fix. The next one won't announce itself either. Register now for GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning, pick the session time that works for you, and find out what your pins aren't telling you.

11we243.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 17, 2026Vulnerability / Mobile Security A now-patched flaw in Apple's audio service let apps on iPhones and iPads record audio even after the user tapped "Don't Allow" on the microphone prompt. The first security updates with the fix came out on August 17. Neither Apple nor the two researchers who found the flaw report that it was used in attacks. Nik Tsytsarkin of Meta Red Team X published the technical details last week. Mustafa Calap, a security engineer who reported the same flaw separately, published his own analysis the same day. On iPhones, an orange indicator shows when an app is using the microphone. On one of the researchers' earlier test builds, that indicator stayed off while the app recorded. In Tsytsarkin's tests, the prompt appeared the first time the app opened. Declining it did not stop the recording, and the prompt did not reappear on subsequent launches. In the earlier build of his technical analysis, the system logs showed no record of the app using the microphone. They named the audio service itself as the recorder. His demo video shows the indicator while the test app records with no microphone permission. He wrote that the video "was filmed on a later build that appears to have restored the orange microphone indicator." Calap's test app recorded while its permission still read denied, according to his detailed write-up. No orange indicator appeared in the Dynamic Island or in Control Center. He does not say which of his two test builds that was. Neither researcher describes a way for users to check whether an app recorded them before the fix. Calap reproduced the bypass on iOS 26.6, released July 27, and on an iPadOS 27 beta. The bypass needed an app already installed on the device. His two test apps were sandboxed apps with no added entitlements. Their only privacy key was NSMicrophoneUsageDescription, which makes the microphone prompt appear. In his tests, recording had to start while the app was in the foreground. Once started, it continued after the app went to the background and after the device was locked. The background version also set UIBackgroundModes = audio. Both apps were installed from Xcode and never went through App Review. So the tests do not show whether App Review would have stopped such an app. The Meta analysis compared two iOS 27 test builds. Neither researcher reports testing macOS, tvOS, watchOS, or visionOS, though fixes are listed for those systems too. The bypass covered microphone capture through the audio service only. It did not give the app other privacy permissions. These releases fix the flaw, which is tracked as CVE-2026-65339: iOS 26.6.1 and iPadOS 26.6.1 (August 17), for iPhone 11 and later, iPad Pro 12.9-inch 3rd generation and later, iPad Pro 11-inch 1st generation and later, iPad Air 3rd generation and later, iPad 8th generation and later, and iPad mini 5th generation and later iOS 18.7.11 and iPadOS 18.7.11 (October 26), for iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, and iPad 7th generation macOS Tahoe 26.6.2 (August 17) macOS Sequoia 15.8 (September 14) tvOS 27 (September 14), for Apple TV 4K 2nd generation and later watchOS 27 (September 14), for Apple Watch Series 9 and later visionOS 27 (September 14), for Apple Vision Pro (all models) The researchers describe no setting that blocks the bypass, so installing these updates is the fix. The iOS 27 notes do not list the flaw, nor do those for later iOS 27 updates as of today. Meta's timeline says the fix shipped in iOS 27.0 beta 5 on August 10. CISA gives the flaw a CVSS score of 5.0 out of 10. The agency's catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities does not list it, as of the catalog's update late last week. Apple's notes for the August 17 updates describe the flaw only as one that may let an app leak sensitive user information. Tsytsarkin wrote: "That description leaves out the most striking part: the app could record after permission was denied, without the orange indicator appearing." In his own tests, the indicator was missing only on the earlier build. An app does not decide for itself whether it may record. That decision goes through the Transparency, Consent, and Control (TCC) system, which checks which process is asking. The audio service, called audiomxd, accepted the app's own word about which process was asking. An audit token identifies a process. An app could send the service a token that named audiomxd itself. The service then treated the app as itself. It took a shortcut meant for its own internal audio and allowed recording without asking TCC. The kernel itself provided the app with the details it needed to impersonate the service. The fix makes the service check the real caller's identity, which the kernel supplies. Outside callers now need the private entitlement com.apple.private.audio.client-audit-token-override to replace the client identity the service relies on. An app cannot grant itself that entitlement.

4vhjcc.text: Government sectors in Asia and Africa have been targeted by an active cyber intrusion campaign that delivers to previously undocumented backdoors that leverage legitimate services like Microsoft SharePoint and GitHub for command‑and‑control (C2). The activity has been codenamed Operation ShadowCloud by Kaspersky. The Russian cybersecurity company said it identified the campaign in early 2026. "The threat actor behind it is abusing the legitimate MeshAgent utility to drop two brand-new backdoors," Kaspersky researchers Saurabh Sharma and Noushin Shabab said in a two-part analysis. "These implants hide their command‑and‑control (C2) traffic behind cloud services Microsoft SharePoint, GitHub, and Ably, allowing the implants to blend in with normal traffic, effectively evading network-based detections." The modular backdoors, dubbed GraphDoor and GitDoor for their choice of the cloud platform used for C2, enable the download of additional plugins on demand and the execution of shellcode directly in memory to extend their functionality. Traffic between infected systems and the C2 servers is proxied by deploying a modified Erfrp client and Ably messaging service-based plugins. The starting point of the attack has been traced back to a MeshCentral Agent, a legitimate remote access tool that's used for remote desktop control, command‑line access, and file management. The attack is said to have targeted an unspecified Taiwanese organization. The exact method by which the utility is installed on the host remains unknown. However, signs point to the "reuse of a prior infection already present on the network," Kaspersky added. The MeshCentral Agent is configured to contact a hard-coded C2 server ("wss://27.102.66[.]162:443/agent.ashx") and then fetch three payloads staged on the endpoint - A legitimate binary used for DLL sideloading (start.exe, pythonw.exe, and zoomit.exe) A rogue loader DLL used to unpack and execute the next-stage malware (jli.dll, SbieDll.dll, python39.dll, WINMM.dll, and libcef.dll) An encrypted file containing the core payload At least two different DLL loaders have been identified to date, each employing its own method to decode and launch the encrypted backdoor payload by injecting it into the current process's memory. "Loader (Type 1) employs a hybrid scheme: first running the data through an RC4 stream cipher and then applying an XOR mask, while Loader (Type 2) simplifies the process by using a straight XOR operation alone," Kaspersky noted. The end goal is to deploy backdoors like GitDoor and GraphDoor, which employ a number of encryption and obfuscation techniques like control flow flattening and nested helper functions to complicate analysis efforts and make it harder to trace genuine execution flow. GitDoor, as the name implies, uses GitHub for C2. It relies on two distinct repositories for receiving command payloads ("/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo") and uploading the results of the execution ("/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Trix"). While the Havo repository is public, the Trix repository is private. The creation date of these repositories suggests that preparations for the campaign have been underway since at least the end of 2024. GitDoor supports 26 commands that allow the backdoor to - Perform file management Log keystrokes Launch a proxy, including using Ably Load shellcode to Base64-encoded Common Object File Format (COFF) binaries and terminate the backdoor The custom shellcode feature is used to download and run different modules that facilitate the following functions - Conduct process injection using methods like Asynchronous Procedure Call (APC) injection Enumerate and manage Windows services List files and directories, wipe file contents, and recursively delete a directory Conduct network-related activity by displaying active TCP connections and modify firewall rules Manage processes, including dumping the memory of the process with a specified process ID into a file and terminating specific processes Execute commands using "cmd.exe" Enumerate, create, and run scheduled tasks Enumeration Windows Registry keys and values recursively and set a value in the Registry Extract user information, along with local groups and its members Add of a new Windows user account or add a user to a global or a local group Record keystrokes to a file ("%APPDATA%\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\Cache\logs.dat") Dump cookies from Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge directly from the process memory using CookieKatz Use Mimikatz to dump credentials from Windows LSASS Capture screenshots of the entire screen or a specific window identified by its process ID Extract WhatsApp's database decryption key Initiate NTLM authentication to an attacker-controlled destination Calculate system idle time and display the last time a user was active on the host using mouse movement and keyboard input GraphDoor, on the other hand, opens a named pipe, creates a directory named "Intel_Log" inside the system's Application Data folder, and gathers system information to send back to the attacker. To establish communications with the C2 server, it authenticates with a malicious application using "login.microsoftonline.com" on port 443 and uses the access token to communicate with the Microsoft Graph API and ultimately stage the data on the SharePoint drive. The malware then fetches three plugin modules from the server and launches them in parallel to carry out screenshot capture, process listing, and keylogging. It also proceeds to reestablish contact with the SharePoint website to retrieve the commands to be executed on the machine. The complete list of plugins supported by GraphDoor is as follows - kl.ts, to log keystrokes at "%APPDATA%\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\Cache\logs.dat" pr.ts, to list running processes scr.ts, to take screenshots of the window that matches a supplied process ID and save them as JPEG images moveDir.ts, to move the legitimate executable, the malicious loader DLL, and the encrypted backdoor file to specific target path channel.ts, to launch the proxy abchannel.ts, to use the Ably messaging service to proxy traffic ab2channel.ts, a covert SOCKS5 proxy that tunnels TCP traffic through Ably's Pusher‑compatible WebSocket service In addition, GraphDoor's custom shellcode capability expands on GitDoor to support two additional commands that allow it to run commands using "cmd.exe," as well as MZ executables. The identity of the threat actor behind the campaign is unknown, but Kaspersky said it shares some degree of overlap with a China-nexus activity that Sophos tracks under the moniker Bronze Sandcastle. Tactical similarities have been observed with prior campaigns undertaken by FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle (aka BlackTech). "On several victim systems, these groups shared the same staging directories as the GitDoor backdoor, with their implants deployed within a one-day window of GitDoor deployment," the company concluded. "While this does not prove a direct link, it suggests that a Chinese-speaking group may be developing and/or utilizing the GitDoor and GraphDoor backdoors." "By using cloud-based storage and messaging services, the actors blend in with normal traffic (as cloud API calls to Microsoft Graph, GitHub, and Ably are indistinguishable from legitimate enterprise usage, evading many network-based detections), and enable dynamic payload delivery, where on-demand plug-ins and shellcode are retrieved from cloud repositories, allowing for rapid updates and functional extensions without modifying host files."

1c9usv3.text: Microsoft is testing a new feature that lets enterprise IT administrators remotely lock stolen or lost Windows devices without wiping them. Named Remote Lock, this new feature is shipping to devices upgraded to Windows 11 Insider Preview builds in the Beta (Build 26320.10003) and Experimental (Build 26340.10013) channels. Admins can use Microsoft Intune custom configuration profiles to lock Microsoft Entra-joined, hybrid-joined, or MDM-enrolled devices that run Windows Enterprise, Education, or Pro. After the IT department remotely locks the device, the system can only be unlocked via Intune, since PINs, passwords, local admins, or web sign-ins will no longer work. Microsoft added that the user's credentials will remain valid and can still be used to sign into other devices that haven't been locked. "Windows signs out every active session, hides all sign-in options and shows a locked screen," said Windows Insider communications lead Stephen Lines. "Nothing is erased: the device stays enrolled and managed, BitLocker stays on and user data stays in place. The lock holds across restarts and while offline, and only an admin can lift it remotely, so the user picks up where they left off." Admins can lock a device from the Intune admin center using the following procedure: Go to Devices > Windows > Configuration > Create > New policy. Choose Windows 10 and later, then Templates > Custom. Name the profile (for example, Remote lock - ON) and add the settings below, with LockState = 1. Assign the profile to a device group reserved for locked devices. To lock a device, add it to that group; the lock applies at the device's next check-in. To unlock, create a second profile with LockState set to 0 and assign it to an unlock group. Move the device from the lock group to the unlock group. After Remote Lock is enabled, the device is not isolated from the enterprise network or erased. To do that, admins must use the device isolation and wipe controls in Intune. However, users must keep BitLocker enabled to protect their data if the device is reimaged or the drive is removed because the Windows Recovery Environment, Safe Mode, and booting from USB or other media are not blocked. With these Windows 11 preview builds, Microsoft has also begun testing new advanced security key management features that let users view and manage passkeys stored on a FIDO2 (Fast Identity Online 2) security key individually. These new features allow admins to configure enterprise settings such as always-required user verification, minimum PIN length, and enterprise attestation. In August, Microsoft also announced new privacy controls that let Windows 11 users choose which desktop apps can access their microphone, camera, and precise location. 1f1xh75.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 17, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Data Privacy Apple on Monday introduced new controls that allow Mac users to give more granular access to data they give to apps, including those that use artificial intelligence (AI) agents. The changes, currently previewed in macOS 27.3 beta 2, relate to increased transparency and more options for two of its APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access. "Before granting an app such extraordinary access, users should understand that it puts all of the data on their Mac at risk," Apple said in a statement. "These changes are designed to help them do that and to empower them to make informed decisions about their own data and privacy." To that end, Device Control and Data Access is being split into two settings: System & App Protection Override and Accessibility. Other changes include - A single method for granting permissions by selecting the requesting app from a list Encouraging users to grant access to just the specific apps (for System & App Protection Override) or folders (for Full Disk Access) that are required for their workflows Increased visibility into the range of data that apps will receive access to or have control over when users grant full permissions An option for users to configure apps to ask every time they require access A transparency indicator when one app is controlling another app using System & App Protection Override Apple stressed that app permissions previously granted by users will remain intact, adding that developers should be prepared to make changes to their onboarding workflows to ensure their apps can handle scenarios where access is granted to only a limited set of folders or apps via these APIs. In addition, apps that use Full Disk Access for disk backup or the new Accessibility settings for assistive technologies can request entitlements to offer the same experience for new installations that they offered before macOS 27.3. "Currently, known apps aren't affected and will keep the same experience without an entitlement," the tech giant added. "Additional entitlement details will be available soon." The development comes a little over a month after Apple began taking steps to tighten controls around a macOS setting called Full Disk Access (FDA) due to security risks posed by artificial intelligence (AI) agents.

gggmv9.text: US District Judge Jessica Clarke has acquitted two brothers accused of stealing $25 million in cryptocurrency in about 12 seconds through a scheme that exploited a bug in the Ethereum blockchain. Clarke's decision comes one year after a mistrial in the same case, after jurors failed to agree on whether to convict or acquit former Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) students Anton Peraire-Bueno and James Peraire-Bueno in this first-of-its-kind scheme, as Reuters first reported. "The question before the Court is not whether the Peraire-Buenos' conduct was right or moral, or even whether it violated uncharged crimes. It is simply whether the evidence at trial, construed in a light most favorable to the Government, could support wire fraud and related convictions in this case," the federal judge said. "Because the Government failed to prove that the Peraire-Buenos made any material misrepresentations in the execution of their scheme, the motion is granted, and a judgment of acquittal is entered for Anton Peraire-Bueno and James Peraire-Bueno." The Peraire-Bueno brothers were arrested in Boston and New York in May 2024 on wire fraud and money laundering charges and were facing 20 years in prison for each count if convicted. According to prosecutors, the brothers allegedly manipulated blockchain transaction validation processes by accessing pending private transactions, altering them, obtaining victims' cryptocurrency, and rejecting requests to return the stolen funds. The indictment claimed they learned their victims' trading behaviors while preparing the attack (starting in December 2022) and took measures to hide the stolen proceeds and their identities. They were also accused of using multiple cryptocurrency addresses and foreign exchanges and setting up shell companies. After the attack, they also allegedly moved the stolen crypto assets through a series of transactions to obscure their source and ownership. The prosecutors also said that, while planning and executing the attack, the brothers deployed a series of "bait transactions" designed to identify "victim traders," exploited a vulnerability in the MEV-Boost relay code, causing the relay to release the full content of a proposed block prematurely, and reordered the proposed block to their advantage. In the next stage of the scheme, they allegedly reordered the block on the Ethereum blockchain, which resulted in the theft of approximately $25 million in cryptocurrency from the victim traders. Throughout the process, the brothers also allegedly searched online for information on carrying out the attack, concealing their involvement in the Ethereum exploit, and laundering the criminal proceeds through cryptocurrency exchanges with lax verification procedures. Prosecutors also said they hired attorneys with expertise in cryptocurrency, extradition procedures, and the crimes outlined in the indictment. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 11h43xz.text: Ride-hailing company Uber is notifying nearly 150,000 drivers that attackers stole their data after breaching AI infrastructure provider Fireworks in early October. In breach notification letters sent to affected individuals on November 10, Uber said threat actors accessed their personal information after breaching an Uber account with a third-party service provider. While Uber didn't share the total number of affected drivers in these letters, it revealed in a filing with Maine's Office of the Attorney General that the data breach has exposed the information of 149,346 drivers, including their names, driver’s license numbers, dates of birth, and addresses. After being informed of the breach, Uber launched an investigation and severed data connections with the service provider to block further malicious access to its data. "On October 9, 2026, a service provider notified Uber that an unauthorized third party had compromised the service provider's internal credentials and used them to access Uber's account with the service provider," Uber said. "After being notified of this incident, Uber immediately severed data connections with the service provider and launched an investigation. On October 13, 2026, our investigation determined that the unauthorized party had used the compromised credentials to access Uber data connected to the service provider." Although the company didn't directly name the hacked service provider, TechCrunch first reported that the Uber data breach stems from an October 24 security incident at AI training provider Fireworks, which was hacked after a third-party cloud provider hack. Fireworks has attributed the attack to a financially motivated cybercriminal threat actor group linked to a series of large language model hijacking (LLMjacking) attacks. The Fireworks breach also led to security incidents at AI coding platform Cursor and digital workspace platform Notion, which also reported that the attackers stole data from a limited number of customers and (in Cursor's case) infected users' devices with backdoor malware. An Uber spokesperson was not immediately available for comment when BleepingComputer reached out for more information about the data breach. The company disclosed another data breach in December 2022 after a threat actor leaked IT asset information, employees' email addresses, and corporate reports stolen from third-party service provider Teqtivity. Uber previously confirmed that hackers who breached some of its systems in October 2016 stole data from 50 million users and 7 million drivers, and that the Lapsus$ extortion group also hacked it in September 2022 in an MFA fatigue attack using the stolen credentials of an Uber EXT contractor. 2u47ib.text: A Kazakh national has been extradited from Italy to face charges alleging he targeted US schools, hospitals, and healthcare entities in ransomware attacks. 43-year-old Roman Khlynovskiy, who was arrested in July 2025 while on vacation with his family in Rimini, Italy, is believed to be a member of the "8-Digits Team" ransomware group, known for its affiliation with the INC and Lynx ransomware operations. Together with his accomplices, Khlynovskiy is believed to have extorted victims in at least six US states (including hospitals and schools) after breaching their networks and stealing sensitive data. After exfiltrating data from victims' compromised systems, they pressured them to pay the ransoms by threatening to release the stolen files online. "The conspirators boasted that they possessed over 50 terabytes of data consisting of more than 70 million confidential health records," the Department of Justice said. "The conspirators also threatened to publicize this highly sensitive medical information to increase pressure on victims to pay ransom demands. The coconspirators' actions resulted in over $500 million in ransom demands." Khlynovskiy faces up to 27 years in prison if convicted of conspiracy to commit computer fraud, identity theft, wire fraud, extortion, money laundering, and threats to disclose non-consensual intimate images. INC Ransom and Lynx ransomware operations The INC Ransom cybercrime gang, whose leak site lists over 1,000 victims, emerged as a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation in July 2023. Its victims include many education, healthcare, government, and industrial entities, such as Scotland's National Health Service (NHS), Yamaha Motor Philippines, Pennsylvania's Office of the Attorney General, food retail giant Ahold Delhaize, and the US division of Xerox Business Solutions (XBS). Lynx ransomware, which surfaced in July 2024, is believed to be a rebrand of INC ransomware rather than a new extortion group and has added over 400 victims to its dark web leak site since then. The group's operators have used an encryptor likely based on the source code of INC Ransom malware, which was allegedly put up for sale on the Exploit and XSS hacking forums for $300,000 in May 2024. ​ However, this could also be a rebranding effort to help the INC Ransom gang operate under less law enforcement scrutiny. BleepingComputer also found in August 2024 that Lynx ransomware and recent INC encryptors were mostly the same based on a string analysis. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 14tp7wt.text: An attacker exploited a flaw in Optimizely Web Experimentation to plant malicious code in some of the scripts that customers' websites load from the service, Optimizely said early today. Visitors to sites run by at least 178 organizations, including CNN, the BBC and Zoom, received the code yesterday, according to Report URI, a firm that monitors the scripts websites run. The code was built to replace crypto wallet addresses with the attacker's own addresses and to capture card details, but the firm cannot see how many card numbers were exposed to the attacker. The vendor says it has fixed the flaw and removed the code. On iPhones and iPads, the code was also set up to load a second stage that the firm identifies as an iOS exploit kit, but it reports no iPhones actually being taken over. In an incident notice posted at 01:02 UTC, Optimizely said the attacker had "exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation" and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. The vendor has also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and added protections to stop unauthorized code from being delivered. The notice does not say how the flaw worked, how many projects were changed, when the fix went in, whether the attacker still has any access, or what customers should do. Smartsheet's script was cleaned once and then re-infected with a hidden version of the code, which indicates the attacker still had access at that point, according to the firm. Writing before the notice appeared, the firm said it did not know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: "That's for Optimizely to explain." Sites that use the service to run experiments on their pages load a script from the vendor, called a snippet. The snippet updates itself whenever the customer changes a setting, according to the vendor's snippet documentation. Each time it loads, it runs a field of custom code called Project JavaScript. The attacker wrote a loader into the Project JavaScript of customer projects and left the rest of each snippet untouched, Report URI said in its technical analysis. The snippets were still served from cdn.optimizely.com with the vendor's own certificate, so every page that loaded one also ran the loader. Some sites serve the snippet from their own domain, and those were affected too, because the content comes from the same project. The loader came in three versions. Most snippets loaded 1688360[.]cc/track.js directly, one version hid that address in base64 so a text search for the domain would miss it, and another carried a full copy of the payload that runs if the domain is blocked. Cynet, whose endpoint detection flagged browser connections to the attacker's server, traced the loader to a file served from cdn.optimizely.com in an endpoint investigation. Its researchers also captured the code on CNN and Zoom pages. A site that delivered the code has not necessarily had its own systems compromised, the researchers say. The firm checked 1,611 Optimizely snippets, mostly identified through its own crawl data, and found code in 188 of them, belonging to 178 organizations. It says the real number is likely higher because it could only check the snippets it found in time. Its post lists all 178, with their domains. Besides CNN, the BBC and Zoom, the infected snippets belonged to Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock, among others. The vendor's own main site and login page also carried the code. Some researchers call the campaign OPTIMJACK. The first injection was seen at 04:21 UTC yesterday, in the BBC's snippet. A mass cleanup began at about 20:40 UTC, and by 21:52 UTC only TalkTalk's snippet still carried the code. That first injection loaded webshell[.]lol, which the firm calls the same actor's injector. The injector had also been planted through Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and Minute Media scripts since late last week, and it first appeared on Turkish sites on September 17. The payload, a file called track.js, replaces valid crypto wallet addresses with the attacker's in page text, forms, links, the clipboard and outgoing requests. It swaps only an address that passes its chain's checksum and sits near a payment word such as wallet, deposit or send, according to a payload analysis by StepSecurity. Copying is not safe either: an address a visitor copies from one of these pages may already be the attacker's by the time it is pasted into a wallet. A card skimmer, added at 13:43 UTC, captures the card number, expiry date, and CVV when they are submitted via the site's form fields and sends them to the attacker's server. It cannot read cards entered in a cross-origin payment iframe, such as Stripe's hosted fields or Adyen's. The code sends the visitor's cookies and a screenshot of the page to the attacker only after it swaps an address near wallet or payment wording. It cannot read cookies marked HttpOnly. The firm identifies the iOS exploit kits as Coruna and DarkSword, as documented by Google researchers. The Coruna exploit kit targets iOS 13.0 to 17.2.1, and the DarkSword exploit kit targets iOS 18.4 to 18.7. On iPhones and iPads, the code loads a script called boot.js from two .icu domains. That script reads the iOS version and opens an exploit chain in a hidden iframe: Coruna for iOS 13 to 17, DarkSword for iOS 18, and, for iOS 26, a separate chain that so far only collects details about the device. Between 17:13 and 17:57 UTC, the attacker also added a Coruna iframe to every visit from iOS 18.6 or earlier. Those pages reload every 60 seconds to retry the exploit, a sign a visitor could notice. The kit's own comments mark iOS 18.7.3 and later, and iOS 26.3 and later, as patched, according to the firm. Cynet's researchers retrieved the second stage using an emulated iPhone browser and describe what they saw as conditional delivery, "not a successful compromise of a physical iPhone or iPad." The firm says crypto has already been stolen. As of 19:25 UTC yesterday, the attacker's wallets had received about $7,040, all within roughly nine hours. StepSecurity put the total across the same addresses at about $6,600. Two of the addresses were already in use before the injections began, and its analysts wrote that "the chain does not show which transfers came from victims." What Site Owners and Visitors Should Check Report URI recommends these checks for sites that use Optimizely Web Experimentation: Open the Project JavaScript in every project and the custom code in every experiment, and look for 1688360, atob( or any script you did not write. The atob( check finds the base64 version of the loader. Review which users, API tokens and integrations can write to your account, and rotate their credentials. If your own forms take card details, treat cards entered on Monday as possibly exposed. Treat session tokens or other secrets kept in cookies without the HttpOnly flag as exposed, and rotate them. Deploy a Content Security Policy with a strict script-src and connect-src. Allowing cdn.optimizely.com does not help, because the code came from that host, and strict-dynamic or unsafe-eval let the payload run on some sites. Consider telling your customers that your site served them the code. The firm kept a copy of every infected snippet, with hashes and timestamps, and could share them with affected organizations and CERTs (computer emergency response teams) on request. For anyone who visited an affected site on Monday, the firm advises: Update iPhones and iPads to iOS 18.7.3 or later, or iOS 26.3 or later. Compare any crypto payment made that day with the address you meant to pay. If the two differ, the address may have been swapped. If you paid by card on one of the sites, watch your card statements. A snippet that is clean now may still have served the code on Monday. StepSecurity also advises: Block the indicators below, and search logs back to 08:00 UTC on Monday. Fetch every snippet you serve, search it for 1688360, .icu and track.js, and record its Last-Modified header. Ask Optimizely which of your project IDs were changed, and when and how. Keep third-party tags off checkout pages, and take card details through the payment provider's own fields in a cross-origin iframe. Replace any card entered on an affected site on Monday, and check wallet addresses on a hardware wallet's screen rather than against copied text. Consider having iPhones and iPads on iOS 18.6 or earlier that visited affected sites checked for signs of compromise. Cynet treats cdn.optimizely.com as a legitimate delivery host rather than an indicator, and it advises against broad blocks of that host or of the affected news sites. The payload changed multiple times during the day, so a single file hash will not capture every version. These indicators come from the researchers' published lists: Domain: 1688360[.]cc, the payload host, with the paths /track.js, /card.php and /hit.php IP: 136.113.106[.]136, the address 1688360[.]cc pointed to Domain: 5vobauua3ojpklx[.]icu, iOS stage Domain: eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu, iOS stage Domain: webshell[.]lol, the injector loaded by the first injection, seen at 04:21 UTC on Monday SHA-256: f7b84b9a94f749f8ced3f0112d0a66894e8bbc3b4aa5592021d1b8976a9bad40, final version of track.js SHA-256: 617df364120adc47fb4f55dcc0c69a9b6c9e108a92c60bc2b64a266254ab02f3, earliest captured version of track.js

5cl0ni.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 17, 2026Endpoint Security / Vulnerability ConnectWise on Monday said it completed its investigation into unauthorized access targeting partner ScreenConnect environments, and recommended customers to ensure that the technician client is running version 26.6.5 or later. The company said additional activity targeting on-premises environments continues to be reported where the identified third-party extensions remain enabled, and ScreenConnect has not been updated to the latest version. "On-premises partners must immediately disable the identified extensions and update ScreenConnect to the latest supported version," the company said. It's worth noting that version 26.6.5 addresses a critical-severity flaw in ScreenConnect client tracked as CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score: 9.9) that could allow files to be transferred and executed through an active remote session without authorization or Host confirmation in certain circumstances. As highlighted by Huntress and Blackpoint Cyber last week, unknown threat actors are suspected to be exploiting an authentication flaw in RMM+ versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 to execute unauthorized commands while bypassing ScreenConnect's regular authentication controls. The attacks have been found to deploy a multi-component toolkit dubbed SCKit that's capable of spreading from infected customer devices to MSP technicians' computers and compromising additional managed networks by means of a C# module called RelayTrap ("RelayTrap.cs"). Specifically, the malware employs a worm-like technique that exploits CVE-2026-84869 to execute malicious code on a technician's workstation when they connect to an infected device to investigate a problem. There is no evidence this worm-like behavior has succeeded in the latest campaign. Huntress has since said it detected another spike in SCKit-related activity on November 13, 2026, impacting 205 hosts across 41 organizations. "Across the incidents, we saw the new ScreenConnect client being hosted at 185.241.211[.]197, which is associated with 1337 Services GmbH, a bulletproof hosting provider known for previously hosting malicious traffic," the company said. "In one of the incidents, we saw a rogue ScreenConnect client establish persistence via a service called Windows Update Agent, posing as a legitimate system component. The service executable (UpdateConnect.ClientService.exe) was placed in C:\ProgramData\Windows Update Agent (de362a425905bcc4)\ and configured to run under the LocalSystem account." In response to the incident, ConnectWise has taken the step of disabling five third-party extensions, including Labtech Plus, RMM Plus, RMM+, RMM Plus Password Link, and RMM+ Password Link, across 400 partner environments. That said, the presence of these extensions alone does not imply those environments were impacted. The company is also urging partners not to re-enable or reinstall the extensions until further guidance. "Disabling extensions and updating software do not remove unauthorized access or persistence already established on affected devices," it added.

13pms4a.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 17, 2026Vulnerability / Endpoint Security N-able has released a new security update to address additional critical security flaws impacting N-central. Describing N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3 as a critical security update, the company said it includes a number of security patches and fixes that enhance the security of the Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) and Unified Endpoint Management (UEM) platform. "HF3 builds on the protections delivered in HF2 and includes further improvements across authentication and access controls, Agent and Probe communications, file handling, server components, legacy APIs, and user management," the company said. The improvements relate to authentication and access control; Agent, Probe, and appliance security; file and import handling; server hardening; and user management controls. As part of the change, the configuration option for legacy APIs has been completely removed, permanently blocking them. As of writing, N-able notes that both Remote control functionality and Intune integration are blocked. Customers running on-premise N-central deployments should upgrade their servers as soon as possible to keep their environments protected. For Hosted N-central servers, no server-side action is required, as the updates are being automatically applied. "All customers, hosted and on-premise, must upgrade all of their Agents and Probes to the latest version to be fully protected," N-able cautioned. "Agents and Probes that are not upgraded are susceptible to impersonation." The complete list of vulnerabilities addressed in the update is listed below - CVE-2026-129271 - N-central Patch Management Local Privilege Escalation CVE-2026-129272 - MMS3 appliance authentication bypass via predictable passcode CVE-2026-129273 - Audit Export syslog injection allows root command execution CVE-2026-129274 - ServerMMS2 task result submission missing authentication CVE-2026-129275 - repositoryItemGet missing authentication discloses policies CVE-2026-129276 - ServerMMS2 asset data submission missing authentication CVE-2026-129277 - ServerMMS maintenance action read missing authentication CVE-2026-129278 - Take Control audit log tampering without authentication CVE-2026-129279 - Password reset response discrepancy allows user enumeration CVE-2026-129280 - ServerUI SOAP operations missing authorisation checks CVE-2026-129281 - View-only users can set DeviceExecute configuration CVE-2026-129282 - Test email sendmail argument injection, missing authorisation CVE-2026-129283 - N-central custom service import XML external entity injection CVE-2026-129284 - Report Manager and Data Export settings SSRF CVE-2026-129285 - XMPP action response origin validation error CVE-2026-129286 - SIS GenericFiles version path traversal leads to RCE CVE-2026-129287 - SIS repository parser XML external entity injection The development comes days after N-able began restricting certain N-central features and integrations following the disclosure of a new set of flaws tracked as 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell. The shortcomings can allow attackers to run arbitrary code as root and gain SYSTEM-level access to Windows systems under specific conditions. Successful exploitation of 4EverAble2Shell hinges on the legacy API mode being enabled. Because the legacy API has been removed from the latest N-central version, it plugs the attack vector. The 4EverAble2Shell vulnerabilities have since come under active exploitation, with attackers leveraging them to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers. Independent security researcher Sean Bales, who disclosed the flaws, has published additional details for 24 CVEs, stating "these are patched vulnerabilities and should not work on the latest patch."

f4v4zd.text: A supply chain attack targeting Optimizely has led to malicious JavaScript being loaded on numerous popular websites, including Zoom, CNN, Fox News, BBC, Salesforce, and GitLab, exposing visitors to scripts designed to steal cryptocurrency and payment information and exploit vulnerabilities in iOS devices. Optimizely is a digital experience and experimentation platform used by organizations to test and personalize their websites, with its JavaScript files loaded into customers' webpages to deliver this functionality. The company confirmed to BleepingComputer that attackers exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation account signup flow to inject malicious JavaScript into customer projects, causing websites using the platform to load malware. "Earlier today, Optimizely identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Experimentation account signup flow," Optimizely told BleepingComputer. "They used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. We have blocked access to the vulnerable path and deployed a fix. We have removed the injected code from affected projects. We have also ended active sessions, revoked tokens, and reset access for affected user accounts. Finally, we have blocked any code from being delivered in Cloudflare. "We are continuing to investigate and will publish any relevant updates at status.optimizely.com. We have notified all affected customers." Major brands impacted The attack was first uncovered by security researcher Scott Helme, who reported Monday that his team identified 188 infected Optimizely JavaScript files belonging to 178 organizations after analyzing 1,611 scripts used by the platform. BleepingComputer independently confirmed that the malicious script loaded, or attempted to load, on numerous affected websites using scans recorded by urlscan.io, including Zoom, KLM, GitLab, BBC, Scheels, CNN, American Girl, ManageBuilding, Smartsheet, Stamps.com, and Salesforce. Other affected websites include Fox News, Mutual of Omaha, American Eagle, Air France, Change.org, Optimizely, HSBC Insurance, Bitly, IG, and UNICEF USA. Salesforce confirmed it is investigating the malicious modifications to Optimizely scripts used on some of its websites. "As a precaution, Salesforce is confirming Optimizely scripts are disabled across preview and production instances. We continue to investigate and will notify affected customers without undue delay if we identify unauthorized access to their data," Salesforce told BleepingComputer. BleepingComputer analyzed copies of the modified Optimizely JavaScript files and confirmed that attackers had injected code designed to load an additional malicious script from https://1688360[.]cc/track.js. The injected code used several methods to load the payload, with some files referencing the malicious URL directly, while others used Base64 encoding and JavaScript's atob() function to decode the URL. Helme also identified a variation that could execute an embedded copy of the malicious code if the remote script was blocked. Malicious JavaScript injected into an Optimizely script loaded by Fox News Source: BleepingComputer An analysis of the malicious track.js file revealed several capabilities, which Helme also documented in his investigation: Cryptocurrency hijacking: Monitors webpages for cryptocurrency wallet addresses and replaces them with attacker-controlled addresses to steal transfers. Payment card skimming: Searches for credit card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes entered into webpages, and attempts to transmit the captured information to https://1688360[.]cc/card.php. iOS exploit delivery: Loads additional malicious JavaScript targeting iPhones and iPads. Helme identified these secondary payloads as the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits, which target different iOS versions. The malicious script also contains functionality to collect browser cookies, webpage URLs, and screenshots, which can be transmitted to the attackers. Helme's investigation found that cryptocurrency wallets embedded in the `track.js` script had received approximately $7,000 in transactions as of November 16. However, some wallets were active before the attack, making it difficult to determine how much cryptocurrency was stolen during the campaign. Below are the cryptocurrency wallet addresses identified by BleepingComputer in the malicious JavaScript, along with the transaction activity observed as of November 16. His investigation showed the earliest observed Optimizely script injection in the early morning of November 16, although it remains unclear how long the vulnerability had been present or how many website visitors were exposed to the malware. Visitors who accessed affected websites on November 16 should review any cryptocurrency transfers made during that time to ensure the destination wallet addresses were not replaced by the malware. Anyone who entered payment card information should monitor their credit card accounts for unauthorized transactions and contact their card issuer if they notice suspicious activity. iPhone and iPad users who visited affected websites should ensure their devices are running the latest available iOS or iPadOS updates, as the attack also delivered exploit kits targeting vulnerabilities in older versions. Overall, users should also watch for suspicious account activity, particularly if they were logged into sensitive services while visiting affected websites. Update: Added Optimizely's statement.
