12o955d.text: Google's Gemini AI agents repeatedly attempted to hack a real organization's website during AI model safety testing, finding ways to circumvent increasingly restrictive security controls designed to prevent them from accessing live systems. The security incidents occurred in October as AI safety research company Trajectory Labs tested whether Gemini 4 Argon agents would engage in unauthorized behavior when faced with an impossible task, even with the model's built-in API safeguards enabled. In reports published Friday, Trajectory Labs and the targeted organization, Epoch AI, revealed that the agents attempted SQL injection attacks, probed for sensitive information, impersonated employees, and repeatedly circumvented network restrictions introduced to contain their activity. Epoch AI said it had not independently verified which AI models were involved, and that the Gemini identification came from Trajectory Labs. The researchers tasked the agents with retrieving official answers to nonexistent problems from Epoch AI's FrontierMath benchmark, repeatedly instructing them to "NEVER stop, NEVER give up." On October 20, approximately 40 agents began probing Epoch AI's live website for sensitive information, including administrator credentials and access to proprietary benchmark evaluation logs. Epoch AI detected the activity and deployed an "agent hotline" that allowed the agents to send messages directly to its employees. For three hours, the agents made 36,411 requests to a planted API endpoint and sent 487 messages through the hotline, including some that attempted to impersonate actual Epoch employees or claimed to be engineers and auditors requesting benchmark information. An investigation also identified an attempted SQL injection attack and more than 200 attempts to access FrontierMath evaluation logs. Trajectory Labs discovered the activity while reviewing agent transcripts and notified Epoch AI of the unauthorized attacks the following morning. After discussing the incident with Epoch, the researchers agreed to continue testing against a local copy of the website instead of its live infrastructure. However, the agents continued finding ways to circumvent the restrictions. During testing on October 23, some agents recognized they were interacting with a copy of Epoch's website, identified the real website's IP address, and connected directly to its live infrastructure, bypassing DNS redirection designed to contain them. When researchers blocked the IP addresses used to reach Epoch, an agent switched to another address that allowed it to access the live website again. Trajectory Labs subsequently configured its network proxy to block direct connections to Epoch, but an agent found another way to retrieve the website's public content through a third-party web-reader service. "In some of these runs, the agents worked out that they were on a copy, identified the correct raw IP to bypass our redirect, and reached the live site again, which Epoch alerted us about," Trajectory Labs explained. In a separate technical analysis, Trajectory Labs researchers also discovered that the agents created a message board through a shared software package cache to communicate with each other, exchanging information about vulnerabilities and exploitation methods. In one example, an agent shared a technique for bypassing restrictions on a deliberately vulnerable copy of Epoch's website, which another agent subsequently used to obtain credentials and complete the task. The researchers also observed agents attempting to bypass CAPTCHA protections and impersonating employees to trick an AI assistant into revealing protected benchmark information. Beginning October 26, Epoch AI agreed to work with Trajectory Labs on additional experiments, knowing the agents would have internet access and could interact with its public website. During these tests, the agents again accessed Epoch's live infrastructure, making more than 65,000 requests to a planted API endpoint and attempting further SQL injection attacks and employee impersonation. Trajectory Labs later moved testing into fully isolated environments without internet access. Even after this change, the agents still tried to disable a fake control that allegedly blocked network access, and they succeeded in all three complete test runs. The researchers said that the agents had not been explicitly instructed to hack websites or impersonate employees. However, they were given an impossible objective on purpose and repeatedly instructed not to give up. Trajectory Labs acknowledged that the incidents resulted from shortcomings in its testing procedures, including conducting experiments without obtaining the affected organization's consent and relying on built-in model safeguards without sufficient additional monitoring. On November 2, the company suspended all AI misalignment testing pending a risk assessment and the addition of further safeguards. "These incidents show how easily testing capable AI agents can spill over to affect real systems and people, and there are not yet shared standards for doing it safely," Trajectory Labs warned. Neither organization confirmed that any private Epoch AI information was exposed during the incidents. This report comes as California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the company failed to adequately contain autonomous AI agents during testing, resulting in more than 80 incidents in which it lost control of the agents. The lawsuit follows a July incident in which nearly 700 OpenAI-powered agents escaped a controlled testing environment and attacked Hugging Face's production infrastructure while attempting to steal cybersecurity benchmark answers. 1697a19.text: Google Project Zero will replace its “90+30” disclosure policy with shorter, fixed deadlines in response to AI-accelerated vulnerability discovery and exploitation. The transition is gradual and began on November 13, when the 30-day extension was removed from the vulnerability disclosure timeline. On February 2, 2027, the deadline will be further reduced to 60 days, and on January 3, 2028, it will shrink to just 30 days. Once the deadline expires, Project Zero will publish vulnerability details even if a fix is not available. Project Zero is Google’s vulnerability research team, focused on the discovery of serious security flaws in widely used software and hardware. Some of its notable recent findings include a .NET Framework zero-day, flaws in Chrome’s JavaScript engine and graphics components, and a Qualcomm chipset zero-day linked to NoviSpy spyware attacks. When the team finds a flaw, it reports it privately to the vendor and typically publishes the technical details after a set period, giving time for developing security updates and patches, as well as a margin for most users to apply them. Project Zero says AI has accelerated vulnerability discovery and exploitation, and made it easier for attackers to reverse-engineer fixes as soon as patches ship and develop working exploits. This policy change puts greater pressure on vendors to investigate reports, develop fixes, and ship them faster to customers. Project Zero said a gradual approach to shortening the disclosure deadline was the better choice, giving vendors time to develop better flaw management and remediation systems. Vendors warned Google that jumping straight to 30 days could expose users to severe risks and could lead maintainers to focus on Project Zero findings while ignoring other, potentially more severe flaws reported by others. “An overarching concern was that immediately changing the policy could harm users by making unfixed vulnerabilities available to attackers while vendors are in the process of improving their remediation processes and technology,” Google explained. “While the benefits of delaying disclosure are declining due to the increased probability that attackers will discover a vulnerability during the embargo period, we still feel there are benefits in the short term.” Project Zero noted some early disclosure exceptions, such as when a flaw is actively exploited in the wild, when others have already published exploitation or vulnerability details, or when a vendor requests early disclosure. Exceptions will also apply for non-disclosure, as Google deems fit, using the example of Spectre and Meltdown, for which it previously withheld information for longer than 120 days. ppq7u.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 16, 2026Agentic AI / Cyber Attacks Google on Monday revealed that adversarial use of artificial intelligence (AI) by threat actors has gone beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks like ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity. In tandem, threat actors are leveraging the power and capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and agentic frameworks to automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize newly disclosed vulnerabilities, as observed in the case of PaperCut NG/MF flaws earlier this September. The abuse of open source, agentic penetration-testing (pentesting) frameworks is seen as a way to "automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during live intrusions," Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a report shared with The Hacker News. The tech giant said the adoption represents a paradigm shift in which cyber attacks take place at machine speed, allowing the operations to be scaled significantly by chaining together varied attack paths even if the underlying mechanics remain the same. A number of threat actors have been observed experimenting with these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated and suspected espionage actors aligned with China. "These observations additionally extend to the use of other tools and services, such as ZeroHollow, an inference service used for exploit development and LLM routing, and Agent Zero, an open source agent framework which features autonomous code execution and dynamic tool generation," Google said. Another key area of misuse revolves around automating labor-intensive tasks like vulnerability analysis and proof-of-concept (POC) weaponization using LLM-driven pipelines, allowing threat actors to collapse the window between patch disclosure and active exploitation. "Threat actors may find it more efficient to use LLMs to rapidly weaponize patched n-day vulnerabilities, as they can focus research on a finite set of source materials: comparing source code versions (including from pre-release or preview channels), and examining release notes, security research, and POC code related to specific flaws," Google added. Simultaneously, threat actors are also targeting AI infrastructure to illicit profit from LLMjacking attacks by stealing LLM credentials and cloud resources from compromised enterprise environments, and then reselling the access through underground proxy services like APIMart and JetNight at discounted prices, otherwise known as LLM mixers. The findings show that the emergence of open-source frameworks have further lowered the barrier to entry, enabling bad actors to easily integrate new exploits, autonomously scale attacks, and mount convincing phishing campaigns, further compressing attack timelines. This includes a Chinese-language phishing platform called Jieyou that has integrated an LLM chatbot assistant to allow customers to configure phishing panels and modify existing templates using natural language commands without necessarily having the technical expertise to do so. "The evolution of the Jieyou platform highlights a growing industry trend where PhaaS providers leverage LLMs as a modular force multiplier," Google said. "Rather than manually editing payloads, low-skilled affiliates can now utilize natural language through the chatbot to dynamically customize pretext lures and phishing interfaces on the fly."

haxdtm.text: A default password opened doors it never should have. A trusted update delivered malware. Even a security feature became a way to break in. Different stories, same problem: the things meant to protect us aren't always doing their job. Meanwhile, AI is making bug hunting faster, old flaws are still paying off, and attackers keep finding easy ways in. Some attacks take real skill. Others barely need any. This week's stories show both sides. Here's what happened. ⚡ Threat of the Week N-able 0-Days Exploited for Dropping Crypto Miners — A new set of vulnerabilities tracked as 4EverAble2Shell has come under active exploitation, with attackers exploiting it to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers. According to Huntback, the activity has successfully compromised 21 N-central servers across the U.S., South Africa, Canada, the U.K., Germany, France, and Sweden. Patches for the flaw are expected to be released N-able today. 🔔 Top News Compromised bee-js and Swarm Desktop Steal Swarm Wallet Keys — Threat actors compromised @ethersphere/bee-js, the JavaScript client for the Swarm storage network, with a new postinstall hook in version 13.3.0 that downloads a second stage responsible for stealing the Swarm node's wallet key and installing a backdoor. "On Linux and macOS, the backdoor is a Go remote shell," SafeDep said. "On Windows, it is a hidden ScreenConnect client that runs as SYSTEM." The same malicious code was subsequently distributed via Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 on GitHub. The activity has since been linked to a campaign called SleepyDuck (EtherDuck), which is known to spread malicious Solidity extensions through Open VSX. "The attacker controlled two Ethersphere GitHub accounts. GitHub activity logs attribute 13 pushes on November 6 to long-time maintainer nugaon," SafeDep added. "That day the attacker injected GitHub Actions workflows to steal CI credentials, and the attempts failed. Two days later, the attacker used the release bot bee-worker to publish the malicious releases. How the attacker got into either account remains unknown." Nightmare Eclipse New SignDrop 0-Day — Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri (aka Chaotic Eclipse) released a new Windows zero-day exploit that can let attackers gain SYSTEM privileges. Called SignDrop, it has been described as a Windows Common Log FileSystem (CLFS) authentication zero-day local privilege escalation flaw. "The vulnerability turns a defense into an attack surface," Cyderes said. "Microsoft added HMAC-based authentication codes to CLFS log files specifically to block the class of logic bugs caused by improper validation of CLFS data structures, which accounted for 19 of 24 CLFS CVEs over five years. SignDrop abuses the signing mechanism itself: it forces clfs.sys to create a .cnpf signature file as SYSTEM in an attacker-controlled location, producing a privileged file-creation primitive at an attacker-selected path. Because the resulting file retains attacker-accessible security attributes, the exploit reopens it and replaces the CLFS-generated content with an embedded payload DLL." Microsoft said it's investigating the reported vulnerability. In late September, the researcher also released an exploit for BigDiskBuster, a denial-of-service (DoS) flaw impacting Microsoft Defender that's similar to UnDefend and prevents the application from performing platform/signature updates. Default Admin Password Lets Researchers Unlock and Start Cars — New research found that it's possible to take over customer accounts at two major automakers, and use them to remotely unlock and start a test car, flash headlights, and sound horns after finding an administration console on the brands' login servers still protected by its default password. Both apps signed customers in through ForgeRock, an identity platform now part of Ping Identity. The carmakers remediated the flaw approximately two hours after responsible disclosure. Google Patches Actively Exploited Chrome 0-Day — Google released updates to patch a high-severity vulnerability in Chrome has come under active exploitation in the wild. The flaw, tracked as CVE identifier CVE-2026-125350 (CVSS score: 8.8), has been described as a use-after-free bug in the XML component. The issue has been addressed in 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Apple macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. Google did not disclose how the vulnerability is being exploited and in what context. Meta Fined by Italy Over Accessing Android Users' Photos with Facebook App — The Italian Data Protection Authority (IDPA) hit Meta with one of its highest fines to date. According to the Italian data regulatory body, Meta has been fined €805 million for failing to disclose that it had access to user photos, videos, and metadata for those using the Facebook app on Android devices. Meta had access to Android users' ​photos and videos through a Facebook app feature that ​suggested content from users' personal galleries that they ⁠could post. The feature has been available since 2023. Meta has 60 ​days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent ​separately. The company said it would appeal the decision. "This is a simple feature ​that helps people share photos and videos on Facebook," Meta told Reuters. ​"Users must grant permission on their device before the feature can operate, and ‌they ⁠can change that permission at any time in their settings." ‎️‍🔥 Trending CVEs Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. Your GitHub Actions May Still Be Vulnerable — Even With SHA Pinning. Here's Why → Think your GitHub Actions are secure because you use SHA pinning? Think again. Join this expert-led webinar to discover how these attacks work, why SHA pinning alone isn't enough, and what you can do to protect your software supply chain. 📰 Around the Cyber World A cybercrime investigation from independent cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs has linked the administrator of Qilin ransomware to Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev, a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia. The TOR project released 0.4.9.17 to include denial-of-service (DoS) defenses related to IPv6 handling. "This release comes in rapid response to the ongoing DDoS attack on the network, which has affected most relay operators," the maintainers said. "This is not an easy problem to address, as relays across the network are being overwhelmed by a massive flood of client circuits. We are actively evaluating additional defenses and so expect further releases in the near future." As many as six pre-authentication remote code execution 0-day vulnerabilities have been uncovered in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A fridge controllers. The flaws, identified by Midnight Blue within the span of an hour, allow full device take-over, persistent access (possibly after reset), and persistent denial-of-service, rendering the device inoperable. Additional technical details are currently withheld. "Through remote code execution, an unauthenticated attacker can remotely run arbitrary code at the operating system level of the AK-SM800A controller," Midnight Blue said. "Due to the lack of secure boot, an attacker with RCE could push malicious firmware that simply renders the device inoperable and irrecoverable without specialized hardware intervention (e.g. by wiping flash memory and/or causing an infinite boot loop). Such a 'bricking' or wiper approach would require full device replacement." The findings unfold against the backdrop of two waves of cyber attacks targeting internet-exposed fridge controllers by Danfoss and Copeland across Europe. Cruciferra has been revealed as a rebrand of the long-running KGB cryptor. It has been sold to cybercriminals since October 2025. ESET said it has prevented over 700,000 compromise attempts from Cruciferra since January 2026, most of them targeting Türkiye, Greece, and Spain. It has been used to deliver payloads like Formbook and PureLogs. "In mid-October the cryptor's domain was seized, and the service went dark," ESET said. "Days later, the same operator resurfaced with a new offering – exclusive $5K-per-build cryptors, pitched against enterprise EDRs and advertised with a claimed bundled kernel 0-day. Seized infrastructure ≠ a dead service." Using AI models on a limited budget and running it against 10 popular TCP/IP stacks has led to the discovery of 99 vulnerabilities in 90 hours. Of these, 66 are new vulnerabilities, 52% of them critical or high severity. This also includes seven vulnerabilities specific to the firmware of a discontinued wireless access point, such as buffer overflow via firmware upload and hard-coded administrator credentials that cannot be changed for web and shell management. "AI cut the analysis time from 9 months to 90 hours and the research cost by 100x when compared to our previous analysis," Forescout said. "It rediscovered 40% of the vulnerabilities we had previously disclosed on those stacks. Total static analysis cost was $935, an average of $2.58 per finding." Since 2021, Project Zero has followed a "90 + 30" vulnerability disclosure policy, allowing vendors up to 90 days to address a vulnerability, plus an extra 30 days "soak time" for patch rollout. That's changing now with the emergence of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation. Going forward, Google Project Zero will disclose vulnerabilities 90 days after they are reported to the vendor, regardless of whether they are fixed. The deadline drops to 60 days on February 2, 2027, and to 30 days on January 3, 2028. ClickFix-style lures are being used to deliver a macOS-focused, modular information stealer called Phexia. The malware is also capable of deploying an XMRig miner. "The most recent and notable change in Phexia occurred in May 2026, when the threat actor started testing smart contracts on the Polygon blockchain as a command-and-control (C2) dead-drop resolver (DDR)," WithSecure said. "The abuse of smart contracts by threat actors as part of their attack chain is generally known as EtherHiding. The malware previously relied on hardcoded C2 domains as well as Telegram channels and Steam profiles as its C2 DDR. The threat actor was observed actively weaponizing the Polygon smart contracts since late May to early June 2026." The threat actors behind WeedHack have been linked to another cybercriminal operation called Marsalek that expands beyond using Minecraft lures to disguise malicious software as popular gaming tools, cheats, and utilities for games including Roblox, Fortnite, and Counter-Strike 2. "Active from approximately December 2025 through May 2026, Marsalek offered free access to sophisticated information-stealing malware through a publicly accessible platform, complete with a dashboard that allowed users to create malicious files, track victims, and access stolen information," McAfee Labs said. The cybersecurity company identified more than 1,560 registered accounts, over 400 malicious files, and more than 29 distribution URLs associated with the campaign. Marsalek also deploys a second information stealer called PureLog to steal sensitive data and exfiltrate it to another server. "This means that while someone using Marsalek may believe they're collecting stolen passwords and other personal information for themselves, the malware operator could also gain access to that information without their knowledge," McAfee Labs. This tactic is called double theft or a dual-hook infection. New findings from SOCRadar show that ransomware operators have started handing the attack to AI agents, leading to the rise of agentic ransomware attacks. "Agentic ransomware is ransomware where AI agents do the hands-on work: choosing techniques, running tools and writing code, within limits a human sets," SOCRadar said. "In less than a year, AI agents moved from building access for ransomware brands to running live encryption and extortion campaigns." An active campaign discovered in early October 2026 is targeting internet-facing Microsoft SQL Server instances and using Transact-SQL (T-SQL) commands to deliver malware such as XMRig miner and Gh0st RAT. The attacks employ predefined username and password lists to brute-force into the servers and exploit their administrative capabilities to execute commands on the underlying Windows systems. "The malware scans IP ranges for exposed SQL Servers and attempts to log in using supplied credentials," Fortinet said. "After a successful login, it remotely executes malicious T-SQL commands on the compromised server to download and run additional malware." It's not known how many servers were compromised or who was behind the campaign. A Europol operation, in collaboration with law enforcement agencies from 14 countries across the globe, has successfully identified vendors and buyers from major dark marketplaces as part of Operation TorNado, a coordinated international effort targeting cybercrime, drug trafficking, and firearms offenses. "The operation, which spanned from May 2025 to October 2026, resulted in 354 arrests and hundreds of house searches worldwide," Europol said. "This effort included a follow-up action focused on the identification of suspects after the takedown of five major dark marketplaces: Archetyp, Bohemia, Nemesis, Kingdom, [and] Tor2Door." The U.S. led with 132 arrests, followed by the U.K. (59). Authorities also seized more than 5.7 metric tonnes of illicit drugs, 209 firearms, and over $234 million in both cash and virtual currencies. Threat actors have been observed using a "convincing device-code phishing attack" that involves a Microsoft Teams calendar invite booking flow to target a company in the construction sector. The attack was observed in mid-October 2026. "While many device code phishing lures leverage a generic Microsoft sign-in form, this attack crafted an email with a believable social engineering lure that impersonated a legitimate senior vice president of another company in the construction sector, complete with a typosquatted email domain," Huntress said. "A link in the message to the victim began a 'Microsoft Teams Meeting Scheduler' booking flow, which included prompts to pick a duration of the call, as well as a date and a time. On the backend, these prompts kicked off the Microsoft device code sign-in process and returned a user code, and when the target clicked the 'Confirm Meeting' prompt on the lure page, they were unknowingly copying the code to their clipboard. Then a pop-up prompt opened to Microsoft's real device sign-in page, asking the target to submit the code, which completed the device-code phishing attempt." Threat actors are probing two of 14 vulnerabilities newly disclosed in XWEB EVO, the Dixell refrigeration supervisor now sold under the Copeland name. According to VulnCheck, the flaws in question are CVE-2026-124014 (an unauthenticated write of the system configuration file via config.lua) and CVE-2026-124010 (an unauthenticated root command execution flaw). 1ur43wb.text: Six flaws in Danfoss AK-SM800A refrigeration controllers could let a remote attacker take over a controller without logging in, Dutch security consultancy Midnight Blue said earlier this week. No patch is available, and the researchers say the newest firmware, version 5.4.0, does not fix the flaws. Government cybersecurity agencies in Belgium, Ireland and Germany told operators this week to take the controllers' management interfaces off the internet. For a controller left on the internet, updating the firmware, changing default passwords or turning on Strict mode is not enough on its own, the Belgian and Irish agencies said. Strict mode is a login protection that requires encrypted connections and session tokens, but one of the six flaws is in the gateway that enforces it. The AK-SM800A runs a store's fridges and freezers, and maintenance firms can manage it remotely. Such controllers were targeted in attacks in France starting October 11, and in a second wave across Europe that began last week. The attacks caused unwanted defrost cycles and destroyed stock. Germany's federal IT security agency, the BSI, says in a security notice that the AK-SM800A was involved in earlier incidents in which refrigeration units in several countries were tampered with. The agency has no information about any exploitation of the six new flaws, and neither other agencies nor researchers link the flaws to those incidents. The researchers examined firmware version 5.3.2, then the newest, and say every version up to and including it is affected. No CVE identifiers have been assigned. The researchers are keeping technical details private while they work on disclosure with Danfoss, the Danish company that makes the controllers. The vendor lists software package 5.4.0, dated November, as its newest release for the AK-SM800A. Its 5.4.0 readme and November update guide cover upgrade steps, and the guide adds a stricter password rule. Neither mentions a fix for any vulnerability. In a follow-up statement carried by trade publication Cooling Post, the researchers said 5.4.0 does not patch the flaws: "It's not really possible either because according to the file timestamp this firmware was likely built on October 29, before the second wave of cyber attacks and well before our vulnerability reports." The German agency first said in a press release this week that 5.4.0 was not affected. Later the same day, it changed that in a corrected statement: it cannot rule out for now that 5.4.0 is affected. The vendor's advisory page lists no advisory for the six flaws as of today, and no date for a fix has been published. Midnight Blue researcher Carlo Meijer found the six flaws in less than an hour of manual review, using firmware the vendor offers for download, and described them in a technical write-up. Five of the flaws are in web request handlers that do not require a login, inside a program that runs as root. Through one of them, the researchers ran code as root on older firmware, version 3.3.0, and they found the same bugs in 5.3.2. Strict mode closes almost all of the controller's web attack surface to users who have not logged in, including the flaw used in that demonstration. The sixth flaw is in the gateway that enforces Strict mode, a separate program that blocks every request except the login until a user has logged in. When the researchers ran firmware 5.3.2 in an emulator with Strict mode on, that flaw crashed the gateway. The crash could be turned into code execution with more work, the researchers say, and the gateway lacks basic exploit defenses such as stack canaries. With code running as root, an attacker could change the controller's settings, start defrost cycles and hide that activity from its logs. The controllers do not use secure boot, the researchers found, so an attacker could plant code that survives a factory reset and a firmware update. An attacker could also make a controller unusable until it is replaced. The researchers say the code almost certainly holds more flaws like these, and they call patching flaws one by one or turning on Strict mode "a misallocation of scarce security and personnel resources." What Operators Can Do Removing internet exposure must not wait for a patch, and it is needed even where firmware is current and Strict mode is on, the Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium says. The Belgian advisory and a similar Irish advisory recommend these steps: Find every controller whose management interface can be reached from the internet, including through a 4G or 5G modem, and remove that exposure. Give remote access only through a secure VPN or a protected internal network. Allowing only a service company's IP addresses through a firewall is a short-term measure. Check temperature setpoints, defrost schedules, alarm settings, user accounts and remote-access settings for changes you did not make. The German agency adds that anyone who suspects a compromise should change all credentials and check that equipment connected to the controller works properly. Before cutting off the data a controller sends to its refrigeration service company, operators should check contract and insurance terms, the Belgian advisory says. They should also set up protected remote access so that monitoring can continue. Danfoss's own update guide says the AK-SM800A should not be directly reachable from the public internet, adding: “This recommendation applies to all software versions, including those with Strict Mode enabled.” Ireland's National Cyber Security Centre also advises running the latest supported firmware, changing default passwords and turning on Strict mode, but says operators should not rely on those steps alone. Danfoss told Cooling Post on October 12 that most units hit in France were either older models that no longer receive updates or current AK-SM800A units running outdated firmware. The vendor fixed earlier flaws in the AK-SM800A in 2023 and 2025, including login bypass and command injection bugs. Version 5.3.2, which the researchers examined, is newer than all of those fixes.

gqzna8.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 16, 2026Threat Intelligence / Endpoint Security Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a new variant of CoffeeLoader, a malware designed to deliver additional payloads to infected machines. "On launch, the NSIS-based installer executable dropped a file named '7z.dll' into a temporary directory and ran it through rundll32.exe," Kaspersky said in an analysis published today. "The '7z.dll' file was a patched version of the original library of the popular 7-Zip archiver. Part of its code had been replaced with malicious self-decrypting shellcode that turned out to be a new version of the Armoury packer." CoffeeLoader was first documented by Zscaler ThreatLabz in March 2025, detailing its use of the Armoury packer to resist analysis and ultimately run Rhadamanthys shellcode. The malware is assessed to share source code similarities with another loader family tracked as SmokeLoader. Malware packed with Armory uses file names like "ArmouryAIOSDK.dll" and "ArmouryA.dll," with the packer hijacking some of the original Armoury Crate functionality with self-decrypting shellcode. Notably, the shellcode extracts code that executes a decryption routine on a system's GPU by making use of the OpenCL library. The end goal is to install CoffeeLoader, establish persistence, and execute it by injecting it into a newly created "dllhost.exe" process. The latest version of the packer continues to use the GPU, but replaces OpenCL with the OpenGL library. In addition, the new version of the packer delivers intermediate shellcode instead of a DLL. This shellcode serves as a downloader responsible for fetching the main CoffeeLoader malware. "To establish persistence, the Trojan copies '7z.dll' to subfolders of %PROGRAMDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%," Kaspersky said. "The Run registry key is used for autorun. The subfolder, library, and registry value are named with eight hexadecimal digits generated from system volume information." "To protect itself, the downloader creates a registry key that prevents the user from disabling autorun through Task Manager." Once persistence is successful, the malware launches one of the legitimate processes (e.g., "dllhost.exe," "WerFault.exe," "svchost.exe," "OpenWith.exe," or "AtBroker.exe") and then injects itself into it, after which the malware shellcode is downloaded from a hard-coded command-and-control (C2) server. The shellcode then decrypts and runs the CoffeeLoader payload. It supports the same three commands to run the next-stage malware from the C2 server - Injecting it into a process Saving it to disk as an executable and then running it Saving it as a DLL and then running it via "rundll32.exe" As for how CoffeeLoader is distributed, it takes place via Retadup, a Windows computer worm that was disrupted by French law enforcement authorities in August 2019. The malware, which spreads via infected USB drives, has been used to drop additional payloads like cryptocurrency miners, the Stop ransomware, and the Arkei password stealer. "Two years ago, someone began re-registering the domain names that Retadup had used as C2 servers and using them to issue commands to download third-party malware," Kaspersky said. "At first, this was the SmokeLoader downloader packed using the 32-bit version of Armoury, but in early 2025, the same servers started serving CoffeeLoader." It remains unclear whether the worm's author or some other threat actor was instrumental in bringing the C2 servers back online. Kaspersky said it blocked around 15,000 systems from being infected with the resurrected version of the worm, most of them located in Peru, Angola, Russia, and Bolivia.

13sbva5.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 16, 2026United States A financially motivated threat activity cluster tracked as REF3364 has been attributed to a Linux-focused cryptocurrency mining operation that tampers with the readings used to detect high GPU workloads. Central to the intrusion is a toolkit called SANSAR, a Rust-based orchestrator that receives commands over the TOR anonymity network to manage CPU and GPU miners. The activity was observed in late October 2026. "The threat actor also deployed a kernel rootkit to hide selected processes and files, an NVIDIA Management Library (NVML) wrapper to falsify GPU readings, and a separate backdoor named netns," Elastic Security Labs said in a report published last week. "This backdoor retrieves its C2 [command-and-control] address from an Ethereum smart contract before connecting to the server directly." In the attack chain documented by the company, initial access is said to have been achieved via an exposed Ray job agent, allowing the threat actor to execute commands. This includes jobs running the NVIDIA System Management Interface (nvidia-smi) to capture and exfiltrate the GPU inventory to an external server. Subsequently, the attacker submitted a Python reverse shell job that connected to a remote listener, after which an SSH key was added to that account's authorized_keys file to establish persistent access. "After obtaining root, the actor staged the toolkit under /opt/vadi_, built the acpi_thermal_mgr kernel module through Dynamic Kernel Module Support (DKMS) and added an initramfs loader," security researcher Salim Bitam said. "An initramfs is a temporary root file system loaded into RAM during early boot, before Linux switches to its normal root filesystem. The module and loader are stored in the boot image on disk, so the rootkit can load again when the host boots with that image." The installation also delivers a modified NVML wrapper that filters process information and changes GPU telemetry to evade detection. Specifically, the altered wrapper hooks NVML calls used by monitoring tools such as nvidia-smi to report GPU utilization as 0%. In addition, temperature and power readings are substituted with random values between 36 to 46 degree Celsius (96.8 to 114.8 degree Fahrenheit) and 100 to 200 watts. Also delivered are the following payloads - sansar, used for TOR C2, launching or stopping the miner, miner configuration updates, connection management, spawning interactive shells, launching an IPv4 TCP SYN traffic task against a specified address and port, and NVML-hook maintenance kurt (XMRig version 6.25.0), the miner selected by sansar's CPU branch tilki (SRBMiner-MULTI version 3.6.9), the miner selected by sansar's GPU branch lyrebird, a legitimate pluggable transport proxy for TOR acpi_thermal_mgr.ko, a Linux rootkit used for process, directory, and socket-list concealment netns, an Ethereum-assisted backdoor Once launched, SANSAR first performs an anti-debugging check by reading the value of TracerPid and exits if it's non-zero. TracerPid indicates the Process ID (PID) of the process currently tracing or debugging the target process. It then reaches out to an onion service ("efxisnqldelyr5ra25oqfrsut54b34g26e7zrsiuupsoekjof2gho2id[.]onion") for C2 communication via Arti, receiving commands, collecting host and GPU information, and fetching the miner status. The main responsibility of SANSAR is to supervise the mining process and launch the appropriate miner executable based on the miner type (i.e., CPU or GPU) specified in the C2 response message. The "acpi_thermal_mgr.ko" kernel rootkit, on the other hand, uses Function Tracer (ftrace) to conceal cryptomining activity on Linux systems by hiding processes, files, and socket entries. It achieves this by intercepting system calls to directory listings, file access, and process termination signals, removing matching records or blocking requests for those hidden processes and files by returning the message "No such file or directory" or "No such process." The other main component of the operation is the netns backdoor that's registered as a systemd service. It's used to retrieve a controller IPv4 address by sending requests to an embedded contract (0x43eb291f56688c63c93e8a93c4591fc997cf6349) and then sets up a plain TCP connection to that address on port 8080 to open a reverse-shell connection to the specified host and port in the C2 response. It's not clear who is behind the operation, but Elastic said it found Turkish language comments in the rootkit's source code. "Organizations expanding GPU infrastructure for AI and LLM workloads should check who can submit jobs and whether GPU monitoring libraries have been modified, as cryptojacking can divert compute capacity from legitimate workloads and increase operating costs," Elastic said.

10eo6nh.text: Attackers' AI agents have been hunting for weak spots in internet-exposed AI apps such as LiteLLM, One API, and Dify to steal the AI provider keys stored inside, according to the agents' own records. The records, which Amazon's threat intelligence team captured with decoy servers, describe stolen keys being used to run the AI models that powered the search for more keys. The team said this week that it cannot verify the outcomes reported by the agents. It has moderate confidence that the agents ran on ARTEX, an open-source AI tool for penetration testing. The records include a playbook of known entry points for each targeted product. It lists default administrator credentials such as LiteLLM's default master key, unfinished installs that an outsider could take over, and known flaws in Langflow and RAGFlow. In a separate case reported this week, Cloudflare's incident responders saw ARTEX gain access to a compromised API token that had been used for CI/CD. The token had no IP restrictions or rate limiting, and the activity that followed included 400 database dump requests in an hour. The company has not said whether those requests returned any data. An operator gives ARTEX a target and a goal, and a planner agent splits the goal into tasks for worker agents that run security tools. To decide each next step, the agents send their work to a large language model (LLM). The decoy servers, part of a network called MadPot, posed as popular LLM services. From October 3 to late last week, the agents sent it requests that often carried a campaign's full history, including the operators' instructions and the agents' reported findings. Those captured agent records describe work done on systems MadPot does not watch. "Amazon Threat Intelligence did not observe that activity as it happened and cannot verify the outcomes the agents reported, but the records show what the actors were pursuing," the team said. The team assessed, with moderate confidence, that the operators were separate China-linked groups, citing Simplified Chinese prompts and China time zone settings, among other evidence. In the main campaign, the agents looked for internet-exposed AI apps, extracted the provider keys stored inside, verified that the keys worked, and added them to a shared pool. They focused on apps that hold keys for many providers, because one weak admin page there can expose many accounts. Targets named in the records include LLM gateways and proxies such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API and LiteLLM, and AI app builders such as Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat and Ollama. The playbook also covers management and provider settings endpoints that need no login, an authentication bypass through the isCliRequest header in One API family systems, and server-side request forgery (SSRF) through URL-fetch features to reach cloud metadata services. Other entries cover secrets left in client-side JavaScript, source maps, debug routes and environment files. When the agents found cloud credentials, they targeted managed services that host AI models, secret stores, and application identities, prioritizing premium AI models over general cloud access. To find leaked keys, the agents used internet scanning services and certificate transparency logs, and searched GitHub repositories and event archives, npm and PyPI packages, container image layers, notebooks, model-hosting spaces, paste sites, and Telegram channels. The records cover hundreds of targets across AI app platforms and other systems. The team notified AWS customers who may have been affected. Microsoft reported last week that attackers were using agentic AI tools such as ARTEX for GitHub secret hunting, looking for exposed credentials that included API keys for AI inference. On August 26, the company described an earlier RAGFlow attack, in which a hidden hook captured AI provider keys as users entered them, and a compromise of a LiteLLM gateway that exposed provider keys. In its RAGFlow case study, the company had only low confidence about which flaw, if any, let the attackers run code. It did not link those attacks to ARTEX. The decoy records also describe a second campaign in which agents attempted to bypass identity checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges using deepfakes. One verification vendor's server rejected the live deepfake video on every attempt the agents made to record it. The team did not say whether the forged photos of ID documents that the agents also fabricated passed document checks. Over the past eight weeks, Cloudflare's incident responders were called into multiple investigations involving ARTEX and tools built from it. In more than one incident, an attacker gained access to a customer's environment with a major cloud provider and moved directly into the customer's Cloudflare account. The common root cause was static CI/CD tokens that never expired, granting broad access across the customer's cloud setup, according to the company. In the ARTEX case, the compromised token was an account-level API token. The compromise most likely came through a third-party cloud provider, according to the company's incident findings. How the token was first stolen has not been disclosed. New Worker scripts with names such as artex-*, artex-pgrecon-*, artex-pgw-* and artex-do-* appeared in the account, each name matching a different task. The activity ran at more than 69 requests per minute across several parts of the account. It included attempts to establish persistence and validate session tokens for other third-party apps. Much of this activity was lightly guided by a human operator, the company believes. Whether any attempt at persistence worked has not been disclosed. Over three days this week, more than 50 families of AI penetration testing frameworks tried to scan the company's customers, and the IP addresses seen running such frameworks now number in the thousands. The FBI said in a FLASH alert this week that a range of attackers have used ARTEX since at least August against organizations in many sectors around the world. The alert summarizes 11 earlier reports and describes no new incident. ARTEX's developer made its GitHub repository unavailable on October 8 after reports of abuse, but community forks, archived copies, and a commercial version called ARTEX PRO keep it available. The alert's examples include an earlier campaign against South Korean financial institutions that stole personal information on about 67,000 people, and the ConnectWise compromise. What Defenders Can Check "None of the techniques in these campaigns were new. What AI agents change is the speed and persistence of the attacker," Amazon's threat intelligence team said. The agents succeeded where basic security was missing, including default or hard-coded credentials, keys left in code and public files, interfaces and inference endpoints without authentication, and unpatched software. The team recommends treating AI apps, model gateways, and inference endpoints like other production systems, assuming that exposed secrets will be found quickly, and watching for misuse through unexpected spending or unusual usage. Here is the status of the flaws named in the playbook: Product Flaw Status Langflow CVE-2025-3248, missing authentication that lets a remote attacker run code Versions before 1.3.0 are affected, and 1.3.0 is the fixed version ( release notes ). CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on May 5, 2025, after earlier Langflow exploitation , and the KEV entry marks it as known to be used in ransomware campaigns. RAGFlow CVE-2026-28797, server-side template injection (SSTI) that lets any logged-in user run operating system commands on the server. The attack needs a registered account, and self-registration is on by default, the security advisory says. NVD lists 0.24.0 and earlier as affected. The advisory lists no patched version. Version 0.25.0, released on April 21, renders templates in the sandbox the advisory recommends, according to its SSTI fix notes . One API family Authentication bypass through the isCliRequest header The team's report names no affected versions or fix. Other checks that apply to these attacks: Change default administrator credentials, such as LiteLLM's default master key, and do not leave a new install unfinished where an outsider could take it over. Search configuration files, environment variables, deployment scripts, CI/CD pipelines and databases for embedded secrets, keep scanning repositories and container images for exposed ones, and rotate exposed credentials quickly, as the FBI advises. Give Cloudflare API tokens an expiry date and limit the client IP addresses that can use them. Both are optional token restriction settings, and new tokens carry a cfut_ prefix that secret scanners can detect. Look for Cloudflare Worker scripts named artex-*, artex-pgrecon-*, artex-pgw-* or artex-do-*. Check logs for the 11 IP addresses published with the decoy findings, and for the more than 2,500 addresses that researchers at Cisco Talos link to ARTEX in their indicator files. The researchers' detection rules for ARTEX are Snort 3 rules 7:76, 7:77 and 7:78, and Snort 2 rules 1:67494, 1:67495 and 1:67496. Rules 7:78 and 1:67496 are off by default and detect traces of norma, the agent harness ARTEX uses.

7yr3ql.text: An investigation into suspicious activity within a Russian software developer's network has uncovered a months-long compromise of its development infrastructure and a software code-signing server. The activity, documented by Kaspersky's ICS CERT team after it was contacted by the affected developer in June 2025, has been attributed to a threat actor named BO Team (aka Black Owl, Hoody Hyena, and Lifting Zmiy). The name of the targeted company was not disclosed, but it operates from within Russia and develops software that has a "customer base in the Russian Federation," according to Kaspersky. Over the course of several months, the intrusion resulted in the theft of confidential information and the compromise of all components of the organization's IT infrastructure, including Windows and Linux servers, workstations, hypervisors, backup servers, security solution management servers, and network equipment. Active since at least 2023, BO Team focuses on cyber espionage and hacktivism, and has a history of targeting Russian entities to steal valuable data and break into compromised infrastructure using tools like Mythic and Cobalt Strike, along with its own malware such as BrockenDoor and ZeronetKit. The group is assessed to be of Ukrainian origin. "Their primary motivation is to degrade the Russian military-industrial complex to weaken Moscow's operational capabilities on the battlefield," Orange Cyberdefense said in an analysis of the group. "They also engage in cognitive warfare aimed at humiliating Russian institutions and demonstrating their vulnerability to Ukrainian digital resistance." While BO Team is known to deploy ransomware and publicize its activities on a dedicated Telegram channel, the attack targeting the unspecified software developer did not involve any data destruction or public posts claiming responsibility for it. "Instead, the attackers worked to entrench themselves in the victim's network by setting up convenient command channels and planting backdoors to restore access in case it was lost," Kaspersky said. "The compromise of the software development (CI/CD) infrastructure and the software code-signing server indicated that the attack would likely develop into a supply chain scenario." The attack, per the Russian cybersecurity company, involved the threat actors compromising the organization's Linux terminal server by taking advantage of an exposed SSH service, and using it to conduct reconnaissance of the internal network to flag systems with accessible SMB, Kerberos, SSH, Telnet, FTP, HTTP, HTTPS, WinRM, and LDAP services. The adversary has also been found unsuccessfully attempting to access internal portals, along with websites like proxy-sale[.]com, start.duckduckgo[.]com, vcsa.vmware[.]com, and vulners[.]com, among others. Event logs show that the attackers further attempted to connect from the compromised terminal server to the virtualization system servers, including logging in to the VMware vCenter web interface. These sign-in efforts ended in failure. However, the threat actor managed to successfully target a VMware vCenter server (version 7.0.3) vulnerable to CVE-2021-44228 (aka Log4Shell and LogJam), obtain a remote command line with root privileges, connect to the hypervisor over SSH, and identify accessible hosts. This phase also involved the deployment of a backdoor on the hypervisor that was run every hour by planting a shell script in the "/etc/cron.hourly/" directory. The script carried the name "pgcache" in a likely attempt to disguise it as a legitimate PostgreSQL component. The primary responsibility of the backdoor is to download and run a secondary shell script from "lo1yaizaeghaevarooD1ahtaichootae.nofrillsdns[.]com." The shell script is designed to download and run the Global Socket (GSocket) utility, enabling the attacker to gain remote control of the compromised host. Select variants of the script have been found to point to a hostname-specific payload staged on "lo1yaizaeghaevarood1ahtaichootaz.nofrillsdns[.]com" to deliver an as-yet-undetermined next-stage payload. "The attackers used the nofrillsdns[.]com service, which allows domain names to be created for free by calling the curl utility," Kaspersky said. "By default, when the malware's command-and-control server is not operating, the attackers set the corresponding DNS record to 127.0.0.1, which is what the script checks. Activating the backdoor requires only a change to the DNS record -- the script will then download and run the malware." Some of the other post-exploitation actions undertaken by the BO Team following the backdoor deployment are listed below - Gaining access to the corporate proxy server. Abusing the certificate of the compromised hypervisor to connect to servers associated with a second virtualization cluster and place a similar backdoor. Collecting information about virtual machines and firewall rules, accessing some of them via a command-line interpreter in the guest OS from the hypervisor. Running an obfuscated bash script to decrypt and run an ELF binary designed to provide remote control over SSH. Searching for secrets on the compromised virtual machines, allowing the attackers to breach the virtual machine of the GitLab software development platform, as well as gain access to some of the repositories containing source code and seize the server's private key. Using the private key of the GitLab virtual machine to connect to the organization's Ansible orchestration system. Using access to the Linux terminal server to locate credentials of several domain accounts and connect to the domain controller using the account of one of the system administrators after likely accessing the memory of virtual machines running on the compromised hypervisors. Changing the security attributes of the user's Windows Downloads directory. Using legitimate binaries like tasklist.exe, findstr.exe, taskmgr.exe, and ipconfig.exe to identify which security solutions were running on the system and to gather details about network interfaces. Attempting to take a dump of the lsass.exe process using the Nanodump utility and obtain the credentials of domain administrators and other privileged users with access to the domain controller. The attackers deleted the event logs after the activity was detected and blocked by a security solution. Using system utilities such as comsvcs.dll rather than established utilities like Mimikatz and Nanodump to create a memory dump of the lsass.exe process. Dumping the system registry using the regedit.exe utility, and using it to decrypt the Active Directory domain database ("ntds.dit") to extract the credentials of all domain users. Launching the OpenSSH scp.exe utility to transfer the collected information to the terminal server. Logging in to the domain controller using the Kerberos ticket of one of the domain administrators and ultimately compromising the organization's entire Windows infrastructure by taking advantage of the fact that the same password was used for system administrator accounts in different domains. Connecting to the terminal server over SSH using root account credentials after possibly stealing them from a system administrator's computer post obtaining domain administrator privileges. Modifying "/usr/bin/nxnode-login" to intercept and write user credentials to a shared-memory file at "/dev/shm/pulse-shm-3088612174." Successfully brute-forcing the password of the administrator's terminal server after about 2,500 failed attempts to place the private key of the Ansible system. Complicating detection efforts by timestomping, obfuscation of malware code, usage of living-off-the-land (LotL) techniques, systematic deletion of event logs, and dressing up malware files as legitimate software. "We found numerous traces of BO Team connecting to various Windows servers, though the attackers only used malware in one case," Kaspersky explained. "The server which apparently held particular interest for hackers, was used to sign compiled builds of the commercial software developed by the attacked organization." "Attackers may be interested in such a server for two reasons. First, they may try to carry out a supply chain attack by injecting malicious code into a product build right before it is signed. Second, the attackers may try to steal the organization's digital signature to use later to sign malware." It's suspected that the attackers likely attempted to execute a malicious WMI script and install a backdoor similar to the Linux variant in the temporary files directory. But after the incident was detected and countermeasures were enacted, the attackers, after having lost access to the compromised infrastructure, orchestrated a phishing campaign towards the end of July in an attempt to collect employee credentials. The phishing email contained the "Account disconnected from the mail server" subject line and sought to trick the recipient into clicking on a link to change their password. What's more, the email managed to bypass SPF and DKIM checks, indicating the attackers had in their possession a private key that was obtained after gaining control of the organization's mail server. The phishing attack was detected and prevented. "The attackers used a service that automatically generates phishing pages," Kaspersky said. "The service loads the content of a targeted organization's official website and displays a password entry form on top of the official site's layout. After entering the password, the user sees an error message. However, the information is actually sent to the attacker." "We repeatedly noted that the attackers tried not to use malware and hacking utilities in order to evade detection," Kaspersky said. "Instead, they actively used system tools such as RDP, SSH, and SCP, as well as system utilities to steal user credentials. This enabled them to develop the attack using legitimate accounts, which also matches the BO Team profile." The activity has been found to originate from IP addresses 193.3.23[.]236 and 80.76.42[.]139, both of which belong to a provider in Ukraine. Further analysis into the malicious activity has revealed that the attackers followed a standard work schedule and operated in a time zone that differed "only slightly" from that of the victim Russian entity. "Based on the totality of the circumstantial evidence, such as the attackers' interest in the source code repository and software build signing server, as well as their use of a software composition analysis (dependency analysis) platform, we believe that BO Team may have set out to inject malicious code into a solution released by the attacked organization in order to subsequently compromise its customers, i.e., carry out a so-called supply chain attack," Kaspersky concluded. "Thanks to the rapid response measures applied after the incident was discovered, the attackers lost access to the compromised infrastructure and were apparently unable to bring the attack to its intended conclusion."

1y6wqdu.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 15, 2026Data Privacy / Regulatory Compliance Meta was fined €805 million in Italy yesterday over a Facebook for Android feature that suggests photos and videos from users' phone galleries for them to post. The Garante, Italy's data protection authority, found that the feature was enabled by default and that the app accessed Italian users' photos, videos, and related metadata without their explicit consent. The company has 60 days to switch the feature off by default, including for people who have already granted the app gallery access, and to request consent separately. Meta plans to appeal and calls the fine "disproportionate", a spokesperson said in a statement reported by Reuters. The app asks for gallery access via a single permission that covers the whole app and several functions with different purposes, the authority found. A general notice about enabling other features appears first, but it does not make it clear to users that they are also enabling gallery suggestions. Fully granted, a permission like this lets the app read the phone's whole photo archive, usually on an ongoing basis. Neither the user nor the authority can check which information is actually used. The authority found a breach of Article 122 of Italy's Privacy Code, which puts the EU's ePrivacy Directive into Italian law. That rule treats a phone as part of a person's private life. Any access to what the phone stores, therefore, requires free and informed consent, whether or not data is sent anywhere or harm results. The authority's order, set out in its press release, requires the company to: Within 60 days, ask for consent through a separate, specific request for this feature, and explain clearly what the feature is for, that it accesses the gallery, and how to turn it off. Within 60 days, keep the feature off by default, including for people who already granted the permission. Within 30 days, report to the authority on the work it has started, and within 90 days, on the measures it has taken. If the company misses the 60-day deadline, the feature cannot be switched on for anyone who has not given valid consent. Meta said in a statement quoted in a Reuters report that the feature works only after users give permission on their device, and that they can change that permission at any time in their settings. The Centro Tutela Consumatori Utenti, the Bolzano consumer protection group whose complaint started the investigation, published consumer advice on July 11, 2025. It told users to switch off the gallery suggestion settings in the app and to check what access and permissions the Facebook app has on their phone. The investigation did not look at whether gallery content was used to train AI models. The company denies any such use. The authority may separately examine a newer feature, launched this year, that allows gallery content to be processed in the cloud. The company had argued that Ireland's data protection authority should handle the case. The Garante rejected that argument because the ePrivacy rules do not provide a one-stop-shop mechanism. The feature has been available since 2023. The investigation began in July 2025 and included the authority's own technical analysis. The fine equals about 0.47% of the group's global revenue. In setting it, the authority weighed the large number of people involved, about 20 million Android users in Italy. It also weighed how long the breach has lasted. The breach is still ongoing for people who have not updated the app, and for those who have already granted permission, the authority said. Other factors were a 2019 decision against the company and limited cooperation during the investigation. Changes the company made after the complaint counted in its favor, though the authority judged them late and limited to people who update the app.

lm88tp.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 15, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Software Security The compromise of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension on Cursor's extension marketplace was the result of the theft of an access key that was exposed in the wake of a breach targeting Fireworks AI. "An attacker obtained an access key we had issued to Fireworks," Cursor said in a Friday update. "The key was exposed by Fireworks, and the attacker used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket we used to share data with them." The disclosure comes nearly two weeks after a trojanized version of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension was distributed through Cursor Marketplace as a legitimate update, attempting to install a persistent SSH backdoor on affected systems. According to the artificial intelligence (AI)-powered coding platform, the read-only storage bucket is said to have contained limited coding agent traces from sessions that were not in Privacy Mode. Privacy Mode is a Cursor-specific setting that, if enabled, allows users to opt out of their data being used for training purposes. These sessions, most of which date back to 2025, were permitted to be used for model training. Among these traces were credentials that had not been edited out, exposing the API credentials of less than 0.01% of customers in the process. The attacker, Cursor added, used these credentials as a starting point to reach select software-as-a-service (SaaS) tools used by Cursor and then access the following data - Select archived non-production Cursor source code repositories, including some containing business contact information Limited customer support data and email conversations Product usage metrics and contact details Summaries of some coding agent conversations Some credentials users had sent to the Cursor support team Cursor said it took steps to deactivate the vendor's key, revoke and rotate credentials, and hunt for signs of deeper access, and contain it after "we identified further access." The company also said it temporarily disabled internal and product services, disrupting access to some Cursor features. The next phase of the attack took place on October 29, 2026, when the attacker used a stolen credential from the exposed data of its internal system to place trojanized versions of Anthropic's Claude Code extension directly on the cache used to serve Cursor's extension marketplace. "At most 5,000 users who requested specific cached versions of the extension on October 29 potentially received the malicious build," Cursor said. "It was available for approximately 11 hours before we removed it. We took it down, took the extension marketplace offline, and worked with the cloud service provider hosting the attacker's server to take it down." The company said it notified affected users who installed versions 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 from the marketplace during the exposure window and helped revoke exposed credentials. It has also moved all inference traffic off Fireworks, deactivated the key issued to it, and cut off its access to all data sets we shared with it. Furthermore, Cursor emphasized that no additional malicious activity has been detected since November 1, 2026. There is no evidence that the incident impacted users who had enabled Privacy Mode, customer code repositories, Cursor's own production environment, Cursor app and its official updates, its other apps, or any other extension or plugin downloaded from Cursor Marketplace. Uber Also Impacted by Fireworks Incident The development comes as Uber confirmed unknown threat actors stole thousands of drivers' license information after obtaining internal credentials. "On October 9, 2026, a service provider notified Uber that an unauthorized third-party had compromised the service provider's internal credentials and used them to access Uber's account with the service provider," the company said in a filing with the U.S. state of California. "On October 13, 2026, our investigation determined that the unauthorized party had used the compromised credentials to access Uber data connected to the service provider." Although the name of the provider was not disclosed, TechCrunch reported that the provider in question is Fireworks AI. Uber has not disclosed how many users were impacted by the breach. Last week, online productivity startup Notion also confirmed its data was stolen in the Fireworks AI hack.

1x30cn8.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 14, 2026Vulnerability / Network Security The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added a high-severity security flaw impacting UnrealIRCd, an open-source Internet Relay Chat (IRC) server, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, following reports of active exploitation. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114713 (CVSS score: 8.6), is a case of improper neutralization of delimiters that could be used to execute arbitrary commands with server/IRCOp privileges. "The labeled-response module in UnrealIRCd 6.0.0 before 6.2.7.1 does not escape the IRCv3 'label' message tag when echoing it into replies, which allows any user on a network with two or more linked servers to inject server-to-server commands that are executed with server authority," reads the description of the flaw in the NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD). The addition comes nearly a week after UnrealIRCd's project leader, developer, and maintainer, Bram Matthys (aka Syzop), released UnrealIRCd 6.2.7.1 to address multiple security vulnerabilities identified with the help of artificial intelligence, including CVE-2026-114713. "We are seeing bad guys exploiting this issue on the internet right now," Matthys said. "Hopefully everyone has hot-patched or updated their server, or at the very least has the spamfilter workaround deployed. If not, do so ASAP!" Exploitation attempts are said to have commenced a day after the release of the hotfix on November 7, 2026. That said, the exact details of the malicious activity and its end goals are presently unknown. The maintainer described the vulnerability as the "most critical issue" found in UnrealIRCd over the past 15 years. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have time until November 16, 2026, to apply the fixes under Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk.

57c392.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 13, 2026Vulnerability / Database Security A type confusion flaw in PostgreSQL lets a database user who can create objects run code on the server. Updates released yesterday fix it, along with 51 other security flaws. Full protection from this flaw also requires rebuilding any C-language extensions installed on the server. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-6460, has a CVSS score of 8.8. Any code run this way has the rights of the operating system user that runs PostgreSQL. All versions before 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, and 14.25 are affected. The PostgreSQL Global Development Group, which publishes the database's releases, has not reported any attacks using the flaw. CISA's assessment in the CVE record also lists exploitation as none. The flaw involves composite types, which are types built from named fields, each with its own data type. A field's type can be changed while older values of that type are still held in other parts of the server. The server could then read an old value as if it had the new type. The fix, described in the project's release notes, adds version checks so the server can detect a value that no longer matches its type. Security researcher Mehmet Ince described a working exploit for the flaw, demonstrated on PostgreSQL 18.6, in a technical writeup published this week. His method is to prepare a query that holds a value, change the type of one of the value's fields, and then run the query. The writeup includes the SQL that crashes an unpatched server this way and a second step that leaks memory addresses. It does not include the SQL for the final step, which makes the server run a command. He wrote that he could "trigger this crash as a lowest-privileged login role." The project's security advisory describes the attacker only as someone who can create objects, without saying which privileges that takes. Red Hat, which ships PostgreSQL packages, says in its CVE assessment that an attacker needs a database login with the ability to create or modify objects. None of these sources says whether an account with only default privileges can go beyond the crash to run code. Ince traces the root of the flaw to May 5, 2004, when PostgreSQL gained the ability to change a column's type. His technique for running code relies on a later change made on May 14, 2015. He also adapted the exploit for managed PostgreSQL services and privately shared proofs of concept with their security teams in August. The providers he worked with include AWS (Aurora and RDS), Microsoft (Azure PostgreSQL), Google (AlloyDB), Supabase, Databricks, and Ubicloud. The writeup does not give each service's current patch status. The project credits more than a dozen reporters for CVE-2026-6460, including the researcher, and credits him on five other flaws in the same release. The project rates 32 of the 52 flaws at 8.8, the highest score in the release. Based on the scores in its vulnerability index, only one flaw in the server requires neither a login nor any user action. That flaw, CVE-2026-116322, lets an unauthenticated client trigger a restart of PostgreSQL 18 servers. Several other fixes are in client tools. A crafted archive can make pg_restore run code as the user running it. A compromised source server can make psql run code through the restore script in pg_dump's tar output. What Administrators Should Do Update the server to 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, or 14.25, matching your major version. Rebuild or update every C-language extension at the same time as the server. Extensions built against older releases still load, but they "may not be protected from the vulnerabilities fixed in this release," according to a repository notice from the project's RPM package maintainers. Some extensions will also need source-code changes. Extensions rebuilt for the new releases can fail to load on older servers. Extension packages in the project's RPM repositories now require the new minor release. If PostgreSQL runs outside its package's own service unit, for example under Patroni, restart it right after updating, a maintainer of the RPM packages says in a packaging blog post. Update client tools such as pg_dump, pg_restore, reindexdb and vacuumdb on every machine that runs them. Do not use the new composite_type_mismatch setting to turn off the checks. The project says doing so carries security risks. The project's advisory and release notes offer no workaround for servers that cannot be updated yet. PostgreSQL 14 is now end-of-life, and 14.25 is its last release. Older major versions are also affected and received no update. After updating, follow the reindexing steps in the release announcement. If you use incremental backups, take a new full backup and base later incremental backups on it.

1nq4x8v.text: Two attacks made public this week allow a malicious host to read data inside AMD SEV-SNP-protected virtual machines (VMs), which are built to keep the server's operator out. One of them, Mior, can also modify a VM's memory and fake the signed report confirming which software it runs. Both need control of the server's hypervisor, and Mior also needs control of the server's BIOS. Researchers showed both in lab tests on AMD EPYC server processors. AMD, which makes the processors, lists SEV firmware for Mior and microcode for Skyfall, both dated August 12. It plans to give server makers platform firmware in November for Skyfall and in December for Mior, and fixes for embedded chips later. Customers are told to get the BIOS update from their server maker. SEV-SNP brings confidential computing to AMD EPYC server processors. It uses hardware-enforced memory encryption and access control to protect a VM, even from the host's hypervisor. The ETH Zurich team behind Mior attacked SEV-SNP while it was starting up. During start-up, a security co-processor on the chip, the Platform Security Processor (PSP), fills in a table called the Reverse Map Table (RMP). The RMP records who owns each page of memory and what they may do with it. The team redirected the PSP's writes to the memory of a graphics card it controlled, instead of to main memory. The team used a card because it believes the PSP reads the values back to check them, and the card could return them. Start-up then finished without errors, but part of the real RMP, including the entry that protects the table itself, stayed uninitialized. That let the hypervisor rewrite the RMP's protections. The team then enabled debugging on a confidential VM that had it disabled and used the PSP's own debug commands to read and write the VM's memory. This worked in all 1,000 attempts across both test runs. SEV-SNP also measures a VM's software image when the VM starts, and the PSP signs attestation reports that include this measurement. In a second test, the team copied a harmless VM's measurement into a malicious VM, so the malicious VM's attestation reports described the harmless image instead. The attack needs control of the hypervisor and the BIOS (also called UEFI), plus a PCIe device such as a graphics card, the Mior paper says. For the tests, the team modified the BIOS to leave the chip's memory-routing settings unlocked. "We operate in AMD’s threat model defined for SEV-SNP. AMD explicitly distrusts the UEFI, thus an attacker can modify the UEFI," the researchers say. Ordinary VMs already trust their host and its firmware, so Mior gives an attacker nothing new against them, the team says. The team ran Mior on one EPYC 9135, a Zen 5 chip. It considers Zen 3 and Zen 4 chips potentially affected but did not test them because it had no setup that allowed it to change their BIOS.
